Dear Keshni Nand:

RE:     British Columbia Utilities Commission (BCUC or Commission)
        British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority (BC Hydro)
        2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application

BC Hydro writes to file its 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) pursuant to section 44.1
of the Utilities Commission Act and in accordance with Commission Order No. G-58-24.
BC Hydro seeks orders from the Commission:
•     accepting the 2025 IRP pursuant to section 44.1(6) of the Utilities Commission Act;
•     that, pursuant to section 44.1(9) of the Utilities Commission Act, the need for
      BC Hydro to acquire up to 5,000 GWh of clean or renewable energy from
      generation facilities in the province for delivery to BC Hydro by fiscal 2034 is
      considered as conclusively determined for the purposes of any future hearing or
      proceeding to be conducted by the Commission under the Utilities Commission Act;
      and
•     that the Contingency Resource Plans of the 2025 IRP are approved for inclusion in
      a Network Integration Transmission Service update under BC Hydro’s Open Access
      Transmission Tariff.

The 2025 IRP advances several plan elements and associated Near-term Actions to
meet future needs for electricity. In particular, the 2025 IRP plans to:
•     Pursue higher levels of demand-side measures than in the Updated 2021 IRP, such
      as Energy Efficiency Program B and Customer Solar A, which provide greater
      flexibility in responding to various external factors that could cause load to be higher
      or lower;
•     Acquire up to 5,000 GWh of new energy resources by fiscal 2034, and to prepare to
      acquire or build additional clean or renewable energy resources should further need
      arise; and
•     Build two significant BC Hydro system expansions to meet future capacity needs: a
      sixth generating unit at Revelstoke Generating Station and a second transmission
      line to the North Coast.

BC Hydro requests that certain information in Appendix F - Reference Prices and Long-
Run Marginal Costs be held confidential in accordance with section 42 of the
Administrative Tribunals Act and Part IV of the BCUC’s Rules of Practice and
Procedure. BC Hydro has included its market price forecast of the day ahead Mid-
Columbia market, that we used to develop the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan.
BC Hydro’s market price forecast is based on Hitachi Energy’s North American Power
Reference Case and is proprietary. The terms of BC Hydro’s subscription for this
product prevent dissemination to third parties, and as such, Figure F-3 has been
redacted from the public version of this document. For the purposes of this proceeding,
BC Hydro has obtained consent to provide this information to the Commission and on
appropriate undertakings, as contemplated by the BCUC’s Rules of Practice and
Procedure, BC Hydro can make this information available to registered interveners.
BC Hydro reserves the right to object to a request for access to confidential information
on a case-by-case basis.

1    1.1            Executive Summary
2    BC Hydro is filing this 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (2025 IRP) pursuant to
3    section 44.1 of the Utilities Commission Act (UCA) and in accordance with British
4    Columbia Utilities Commission (BCUC or Commission) Order No. G-58-24. 1
5    BC Hydro seeks an order from the BCUC accepting the 2025 IRP pursuant to
6    section 44.1(6) of the UCA. BC Hydro also seeks an order pursuant to
7    section 44.1(9) of the UCA that the need for BC Hydro to acquire up to 5,000 GWh
8    of clean or renewable energy from generation facilities in the province for delivery to
9    BC Hydro by fiscal 2034 is considered as conclusively determined for the purposes
10   of any future hearing or proceeding to be conducted by the Commission under the
11   UCA. 2 Lastly, BC Hydro seeks an order approving the Contingency Resource Plans3
12   of the 2025 IRP for inclusion in a Network Integration Transmission Service update
13   under BC Hydro’s Open Access Transmission Tariff.

14   An integrated resource plan is a guidebook for what, when, and how to meet
15   customers’ evolving electricity needs. The 2025 IRP looks at a 20-year plus
16   timeframe and will guide decisions on our integrated system to meet our customer’s
17   evolving demand for electricity.



     1   The 2025 IRP meets the requirements of the UCA and the Clean Energy Act and is presented in accordance
         with the updated BCUC Resource Planning Guidelines and areas of focus identified in the BCUC’s decision
         on the Updated 2021 IRP. It incorporates applicable Commission requirements and requests, as further
         detailed in the chapters that follow.
     2   BC Hydro submits that there is sufficient information available in the 2025 IRP to enable the BCUC to make
         this determination under section 44.1(9) of the UCA. This information is provided in section 3.3. As part of
         the Public Notice for this proceeding, BC Hydro proposes to provide notice to parties that may be directly
         affected by this determination which include the following: all members of the TAC, all Indigenous Nations
         and Tribal Councils in BC and the FNEMC, all stakeholders who actively participated in the Updated
         2021 IRP and BC Hydro’s Public and Customer engagement streams for the 2025 IRP, municipalities and
         industry associations. This determination is consistent with a similar determination the BCUC made under
         section 44.1(9) in its decision on BC Hydro’s Updated 2021 IRP which BC Hydro submits was successful at
         promoting regulatory efficiency without unduly expanding the scope of review of the Updated 2021 IRP.
         BC Hydro expects that the determination we are seeking in this 2025 IRP would have a similar benefit.
     3   Contingency Resource Plans are defined in Attachment P of BC Hydro’s Open Access Transmission Tariff
         as the high load forecast scenario and resource plan contingencies approved by the BCUC. For the
         2025 IRP, these include the High Load Scenario, the North Coast Load Sensitivity, and all the IRP elements
         related to Network Resources, i.e. electricity generation, as per BC Hydro’s Open Access Transmission
         Tariff.

1    The 2025 IRP is informed by BC Hydro’s current planning context where geopolitical
2    instability and shifting trade relationships, changing economic conditions,
3    technological advancements and climate variability are all contributing to uncertain
4    load and supply outlooks. Similar to the Updated 2021 IRP 4, reconciliation with First
5    Nations, climate action and electrification continue to be public policy priorities,
6    which have informed the 2025 IRP.

7    An emerging public policy priority informing the 2025 IRP is the provincial and
8    federal governments’ focus on diversifying the economy and trade. To support this
9    priority, both governments have introduced legislation to streamline approval
10   processes to get major projects built faster. The impact of these projects is reflected
11   in the 2025 IRP, particularly in the North Coast region and in certain investments
12   advanced by this plan such as another Call for Power, the North Coast Transmission
13   Line and the addition of a sixth unit at the Revelstoke Generating Station.

14   BC Hydro’s commitment to reconciliation with First Nations informed the 2025 IRP. A
15   consultation process occurred throughout the development of the 2025 IRP, and
16   final feedback showed a strong desire for early and meaningful engagement in
17   BC Hydro’s planning, emphasizing inclusion, environmental protection, local
18   economic benefits, and clean energy solutions. First Nations also highlighted the
19   importance of keeping pace with evolving energy technologies and customer needs
20   and advancing social equity through community-led energy projects and maintaining
21   transparent, ongoing dialogue.

22   We reviewed the planning objectives used for the Updated 2021 IRP considering our
23   current planning context and determined that the objectives remain appropriate for
24   the 2025 IRP. They are:

25   •     supporting the growth of B.C.’s economy,




     4   Updated 2021 IRP refers to the complete evidentiary record of the 2021 IRP proceeding.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                    Page 1-2
                                                                          Executive Summary




1    •    keeping costs down for customers,

2    •    reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions through clean electricity, and

3    •    limiting land and water impacts.

4    The 2025 IRP considers load uncertainty through a range of load forecast scenarios,
5    including a Reference Load Scenario, a High Load Scenario, a Low Load Scenario,
6    as well as a North Coast Load Sensitivity. Load growth is driven primarily by mining,
7    liquefied natural gas (LNG) development, increased adoption of light-duty electric
8    vehicles (EVs), new residential development, and heat pump adoption. The High
9    Load Scenario and North Coast Load Sensitivity include higher industrial growth,
10   particularly in the oil and gas, LNG, and mining sectors. The Low Load Scenario
11   reflects a slower pace of electrification, lower industrial and lower economic activity,
12   and the continuation of historic stagnation in load growth.

13   The 2025 IRP compares our existing, committed, and initiated resources against the
14   range of load forecast scenarios to assess when we will need additional resources to
15   meet future customers’ energy and capacity needs. Before demand-side measures,
16   under the Reference Load Scenario, new energy is needed in fiscal 2031, with new
17   energy needed as early as the start of the planning horizon in fiscal 2029 under the
18   High Load Scenario. New capacity is needed in fiscal 2036 under the Reference
19   Load Scenario and needed at the start of the planning horizon in fiscal 2029 under
20   the High Load Scenario. Growing industrial demand in the province’s North Coast
21   means new transmission to this region may be required as early as fiscal 2033.

22   The 2025 IRP advances several plan elements and associated Near-term Actions to
23   meet these future needs for electricity. In particular, the 2025 IRP plans to:

24   •    Pursue higher levels of demand-side measures than in the Updated 2021 IRP,
25        such as Energy Efficiency Program B and Customer Solar A, which provide
26        greater flexibility in responding to various external factors that could cause load
27        to be higher or lower;



                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 1-3
                                                                           Executive Summary




1    •    Acquire up to 5,000 GWh of new energy resources by fiscal 2034, and to
2         prepare to acquire or build additional clean or renewable energy resources
3         should further need arise; and

4    •    Build two significant BC Hydro system expansions to meet future capacity
5         needs: a sixth generating unit at Revelstoke Generating Station and a second
6         transmission line to the North Coast.

7    Addressing and preparing for uncertainty is a foundational aspect of this 2025 IRP.
8    There is a focus on load growth uncertainty and on how we prepare to meet our
9    obligations to serve load which is difficult to forecast with precision over the long
10   term. This challenge is especially heightened given the long lead times for new
11   supply resources and the potential limitations on access to US markets because of
12   the current trade dispute. Within this context, a “just in time” approach to meeting
13   demand is not prudent.

14   That’s why the 2025 IRP continues the flexible resource planning approach
15   introduced in the Updated 2021 IRP that was accepted by the BCUC. The plan
16   considers the lead time for new supply resources and emphasizes actions that
17   prepare for many potential futures by considering ranges rather than static
18   targets. The plan also reflects BC Hydro’s view that the risks of under- and over-
19   supply are asymmetric. Not having enough electricity would represent a failure to
20   meet our obligations to our customers and could undermine key government efforts
21   to diversify our economy, particularly in a time of geopolitical uncertainty. In contrast,
22   having surplus electricity would result in time-limited financial implications that could
23   be mitigated through flexibility in other parts of our plan.

24   Consultation was undertaken with First Nations and the public though two phases:
25   Phase 1 gathered input on planning topics while the plan was being developed,
26   while Phase 2 gathered feedback on the elements of the 2025 IRP and the 2025 IRP

2    2025 IRP development. Feedback from public survey respondents (comprising three
3    sub-groups illustrated in Figure 1-1 below) showed over three quarters of

5    for our 2025 IRP elements and for the plan overall.

1    Many of these Near-term Actions will require further engagement and consultation
2    and separate approvals from the BCUC. The 2025 IRP will inform the engagement
3    and consultation and the BCUC’s consideration of those applications.

4    We will continue to monitor our planning context and undertake regular resource
5    planning cycles. We expect to file the next integrated resource plan sometime in
6    calendar 2028.

7    The requirements for an IRP are set out by the UCA and the Clean Energy Act.
8    In particular, section 44.1 of the UCA establishes the framework for the submission
9    and review of a long-term resource plan by the BCUC.

10   Sub-section 44.1(2) of the UCA outlines the key components that must be included in
11   a long-term resource plan. Sub-section 44.1(6) provides that the BCUC must accept
12   the plan if it determines that carrying out the plan would be in the public interest, while
13   sub-section 44.1(8) sets out the factors the BCUC must consider in making that
14   determination.

15   In addition, the 2025 IRP is informed by:

16   •      The BCUC’s interpretation of the purpose of a long-term resource plan, which is
17          to "facilitate efficient and effective oversight of public utilities by periodically
18          reviewing a utility’s long-term plans and the choices they face when deciding
19          how to provide safe and reliable service at just and reasonable rates.” 11



     7    Relative to a start year of F2028.
     8    ELCC is a metric used by BC Hydro, aligned with industry practice, that determines the extent to which
          resources can contribute to the capability of our system in meeting peak demand.
     9    The Revelstoke Unit 6 project is exempt from sections 45 to 47 of the Utilities Commission Act pursuant to
          section 7 of the Clean Energy Act.
     10   On October 20, 2025, the Government of B.C. introduced Bill 31 - Energy Statutes Amendment Act, 2025
          regarding the North Coast transmission line project, among other things. The Government News Release
          regarding Bill 31 (see: https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2025ECS0044-001032) states that the Government
          of B.C. will exempt BC Hydro from the requirement to obtain a CPCN for this project.
     11   British Columbia Utilities Commission Decision and Order No. G-283-21, Creative Energy Vancouver
          Platforms Inc., 2021 Long Term Resource Plan, September 27, 2021 (Creative Energy LTRP) at p.5 of the
          Reasons for Decision.

4           which reflect this flexible approach and provide updated guidance on resource

1    2.1            Introduction
2    This Chapter sets out the planning context for the 2025 IRP and the framework that
3    BC Hydro has applied to make long-term resource planning decisions within this
4    context. As discussed further in the sections below:

5    •     The BCUC accepted BC Hydro’s Updated 2021 IRP which contained several
6          elements and associated Near-term Actions, almost all of which are now either
7          completed or on track to be completed. As part of advancing these Near-term
8          Actions, BC Hydro has made progress on its reconciliation efforts with First
9          Nations.

10   •     In its decision on the Updated 2021 IRP, the BCUC identified some areas
11         where it expected the 2025 IRP to focus, including: aligning methodologies
12         across load scenarios, considering specifics of resource options likely to fill
13         future resource gaps, considering options to enhance system resiliency and
14         encouraging communication between BC Hydro and FortisBC on resource
15         planning issues. The 2025 IRP responds to these focus areas.

16   •     For the 2025 IRP, geopolitical instability and shifting trade relationships,
17         changing economic conditions, technological advancements and climate
18         variability are all contributing to uncertain load and supply outlooks. Similar to
19         the Updated 2021 IRP, reconciliation with First Nations, climate action and
20         electrification continue to be public policy priorities, which have informed the
21         2025 IRP. An emerging public policy priority informing the 2025 IRP is the
22         provincial and federal governments’ focus on diversifying the economy and
23         trade.

24   •     BC Hydro has considered a range of load scenarios that set out the potential
25         future electricity needs to be met by the 2025 IRP. The compound annual
26         growth rates for energy from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2050 for these load scenarios
27         range from 1.8% for the High Load Scenario, 1.4% for the Reference Load



                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                          Page 2-1
                                                   Planning Context and Decision Framework




1        Scenario and 0.5% for the Low Load Scenario, before consideration of future
2        demand-side measures. The scenarios reflect varying economic conditions,
3        different paces of electrification, and a range of industrial activity. We have also
4        considered a North Coast Load Sensitivity which captures demand potential for
5        mining, liquified natural gas, ports and other new loads in the North Coast
6        region, above the level of load growth considered for that region in either the
7        Reference or High Load Scenarios.

8    •   These load scenarios and sensitivity are compared to our existing, committed
9        and initiated resources while applying BC Hydro’s planning criteria to show the
10       timing and volume of additional resources required to meet customers’ demand.
11       Following this process, the system energy load resource balances before
12       planned resources show a deficit of approximately 5,000 GWh by fiscal 2040
13       under the Reference Load Scenario, increasing to approximately 13,000 GWh
14       under the High Load Scenario and approximately 14,000 GWh under the North
15       Coast Load Sensitivity. The system capacity load resource balance for the
16       Reference Load Scenario shows a small capacity gap before planned
17       resources starting in fiscal 2036 while the High Load Scenario and North Coast
18       Load Sensitivity both show an earlier capacity need, increasing to
19       approximately 1,400 MW by fiscal 2040. While all three transmission-
20       constrained regions (South Coast, Vancouver Island and North Coast) show
21       some capacity need in certain load scenarios, the need is most pronounced for
22       the North Coast under the North Coast Load Sensitivity which shows a potential
23       regional capacity need of up to 900 MW by fiscal 2040.

24   •   We have updated our inventory of resource options available to meet this need.
25       Key updates for the 2025 IRP include adjustments to cost and performance of
26       demand side measures; capital cost updates to onshore wind, solar and battery
27       resource options, and expanding the pumped storage hydro inventory of
28       resource options to include long-duration pumped storage options.




                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                     Page 2-2
                                                    Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    •    BC Hydro consulted on the 2025 IRP through three streams: a public stream, a
2         First Nations stream, and a technical stream consisting of a Technical Advisory
3         Committee. In Phase 1 of consultation, we gathered input on planning topics
4         while the plan was being developed. In Phase 2 of consultation, we gathered
5         feedback on elements of the 2025 IRP. Feedback from public survey
6         respondents showed over three quarters of participants supported the
7         2025 IRP. First Nations respondents also showed support for our 2025 IRP
8         elements and for the plan overall.

9    •    We determined that our planning objectives for the Updated 2021 IRP remain
10        appropriate for the 2025 IRP. They are: supporting the growth of B.C.’s
11        economy, keeping costs down for customers, reducing greenhouse gas
12        emissions through clean electricity, and limiting land and water impacts.

13   •    Our decision framework focuses on achieving flexibility to respond to load
14        uncertainty, particularly with regard to large industrial loads and to respond to
15        supply uncertainty, particularly with regard to the lead times for new energy and
16        capacity resources.

17   2.1.1       2021 Integrated Resource Plan
18   This section explains how BC Hydro’s previous long-term resource plan, the
19   Updated 2021 IRP, has informed the planning context for the 2025 IRP. It describes
20   the status of the Updated 2021 IRP elements and associated Near-term Actions and
21   provides a summary of how the BCUC decision on the Updated 2021 IRP has
22   informed the focus of the 2025 IRP.

23   2.1.1.1     Updated 2021 IRP Elements and Associated Near-term Actions are
24               On Track
25   The BCUC accepted BC Hydro’s Updated 2021 IRP, which included several
26   elements and associated Near-term Actions, almost all of which are now either
27   completed or on track to be completed. In its 2021 IRP Decision, the BCUC also
28   stated that the Updated 2021 IRP represented one step in BC Hydro’s Indigenous

11   2.2      The Planning Environment
12   In this section, we discuss the planning environment for the 2025 IRP. The BCUC’s
13   Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term resource plan should provide
14   an overview of relevant external factors. 9

15   For the 2025 IRP, geopolitical instability and shifting trade relationships, changing
16   economic conditions, and technological advancements are all contributing to
17   uncertain load and supply outlooks. Similar to the Updated 2021 IRP, reconciliation
18   with First Nations, climate action and electrification continue to be public policy
19   priorities, which have informed the 2025 IRP. Government’s focus on diversifying the
20   economy and trade is an emerging public policy priority informing this 2025 IRP.




     9   Section 1 (a) of the 2025 Resource Planning Guidelines.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                              Page 2-11
                                                       Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    2.2.1         External factors mean BC Hydro’s load and supply outlook is
2                  uncertain
3    Geopolitical instability and shifting trade relationships, changing economic
4    conditions, and technological advancements are all contributing to uncertain load
5    and supply outlooks. Specifically:

6    •    Geopolitical instability and shifting trade relationships: On
7         February 1, 2025, the President of the United States announced tariffs on
8         Canadian goods imported into the United States and soon after, Canada
9         responded with its own retaliatory tariffs. Since that time, various tariffs have
10        been rescinded or expanded and discussions on a new trade deal have been
11        ongoing. These ongoing trade actions have increased costs and uncertainty for
12        some of BC Hydro’s customers, led to supply chain disruptions and increased
13        costs, and prompted the federal and provincial governments to implement
14        measures to support affected industries and diversify the economy and trading
15        relationships.

16        These factors have counterbalancing impacts on BC Hydro’s load and supply.
17        While tariff impacts could mean lower load for some customers, measures to
18        diversify the economy could increase the probability of new customers and
19        loads. Similarly, with regard to supply, while supply chain disruptions may
20        create development challenges for new resources, measures to support
21        affected industries and reduce permitting timelines could have offsetting
22        impacts.

23   •    Economic conditions: While the rate of inflation in Canada has stabilized,
24        previous high levels of global inflation continue to be reflected in the high cost
25        of living and supplies. The provincial and federal governments have advanced
26        measures to support individuals and businesses impacted by high inflation and
27        costs.




                           BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 2-12
                                                      Planning Context and Decision Framework




1         These factors generally increase the uncertainty of BC Hydro’s load and supply
2         outlook. Increased costs could influence customer consumption, impact
3         electrification decisions, or create challenges for capital investment and
4         resource development.

5    •    Technological advancement: Advancements in technology continue to have a
6         positive impact on the cost and availability of certain energy resources as well
7         as energy efficiency and demand response measures. Technology is also
8         helping to enable customers to advance electrification. However, the pace and
9         scale of technological adoption and its ultimate impact on the supply and
10        demand for electricity remains uncertain.

11   2.2.2       Diversifying B.C.’s economy is a public policy priority
12               impacting the 2025 IRP
13   Climate action and electrification, and reconciliation with First Nations continue to be
14   public policy priorities informing the 2025 IRP, with diversifying the economy and
15   trade now as an emerging public policy priority. Specifically:

16   •    Climate action and electrification: The 2024 Climate Change Accountability
17        Report, released in May 2025, concluded that “B.C.’s current policy landscape
18        does not put [the province] on track to meet our 2030 targets.” In response, the
19        Government of B.C. has launched an independent review of the CleanBC plan
20        which includes objectives to review the emissions targets and the pathways to
21        achieve them.

22        While climate action and electrification continue to be a focus for the provincial
23        and federal governments, recent developments across jurisdictions may
24        influence the pace of certain electrification activity, including:

25        o In the United States, there is a shift towards prioritizing fossil fuel
26           development, including lifting the freeze on new liquified natural gas export
27           permits, which could impact the competitiveness of liquified natural gas
28           export development in BC.


                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 2-13
                                                    Planning Context and Decision Framework




1        o In Canada, removal of the consumer carbon tax federally and provincially
2           may impact customer electrification decisions.

3        o Across North America, electric vehicle purchase costs remain higher than
4           comparable internal combustion vehicles, with tariffs in place on lower cost
5           electric vehicle imports, and governments pausing electric vehicle purchase
6           incentives. Major vehicle producers are scaling back electric vehicle
7           production targets in response to weakening consumer interest in
8           purchasing electric vehicles.

9        o At the municipal level, many local governments in B.C. have adopted zero
10          carbon building codes, which will increase the use of clean electricity in new
11          construction.

12   •   Reconciliation with First Nations: The Updated 2021 IRP described
13       BC Hydro’s commitment to supporting reconciliation with Indigenous peoples,
14       recognizing the United Nations Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
15       (UNDRIP) as a guiding framework for reconciliation across all sectors of
16       Canadian society. We acknowledge that the development and operation of our
17       electricity system has significant impacts on the lives, rights, and interests of
18       Indigenous peoples. We also recognize that strong, respectful, and
19       collaborative relationships with First Nations are essential to the continued
20       success and growth of B.C.’s clean electricity system.

21       In the 2025 IRP, reconciliation with First Nations is an overarching
22       consideration that informs each planning objective.

23       Early engagement is a key component of advancing reconciliation, and the
24       2025 IRP represents the earliest stage at which BC Hydro can engage with
25       First Nations on planning to meet future electricity needs. Further engagement




                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                    Page 2-14
                                                                 Planning Context and Decision Framework




1           and consultation will continue during implementation of the 2025 IRP Near-term
2           Actions. 10

3    •      Diversifying the economy and trade: In response to the geopolitical instability
4           and shifting trade relationships, discussed above, the federal and provincial
5           governments are implementing measures to diversify the economy and trade.
6           The Government of B.C. has enacted the Renewable Energy Projects
7           (Streamlined Permitting) Act and Infrastructure Projects Act to reduce
8           permitting timelines for priority projects. The initial list of major projects
9           identified by the Government of B.C. for accelerated approvals and permits
10          were considered in BC Hydro’s load scenarios and the North Coast Load
11          Sensitivity as well as our supply outlook for the 2025 IRP. With regard to the
12          Government of Canada, the Building Canada Act and the creation of the Major
13          Projects Office similarly aim to reduce federal approval timelines for “projects
14          determined to be in the national interest”. The focus of these efforts is on ports,
15          railways, energy corridors, critical mineral developments and clean energy
16          initiatives that are considered in BC Hydro's load scenarios, particularly in the
17          North Coast region. On September 11, 2025, the Government of Canada
18          announced its initial list of priority projects referred to its Major Projects Office
19          which included two projects in British Columbia: LNG Canada Phase 2 and the
20          Red Chris Mine expansion. 11 On, October 20, 2025, the Government of B.C.
21          tabled Bill 31 - the Energy Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 and announced its
22          intent to implement regulatory and policy changes to expedite the construction
23          of the North Coast Transmission Line in partnership with First Nations, and
24          ensure electricity is available for sectors that produce jobs, generate public




     10 Table 2-1 above lists reconciliation efforts during implementation of the Updated 2021 IRP Near-term Actions.

     11   https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2025/09/11/prime-minister-carney-announces-first-projects-
          be-reviewed-new

1           revenues, and have the greatest opportunity to decarbonize, including mining,
2           upstream natural gas, LNG and manufacturing. 12

3    The primary impact of these public policy priorities is that they create the potential
4    for significant and rapid load growth from new projects. While the actual new load
5    that may develop in response to these policy priorities is uncertain, it creates a need
6    for BC Hydro to consider how to advance investments in new supply resources so
7    that we are ready to meet potential future customer needs.

8    However, while we plan for the future, we must also consider current economic
9    conditions. The Canadian economy is currently contracting due to, among other
10   things, the impacts of shifting trade relationships and federal changes to immigration
11   policies resulting in weaker population growth. This introduces the potential for a
12   recession in the near-term alongside the longer-term potential for economic growth
13   from government’s’ economic diversification efforts.


14   2.3             Load Scenarios and Sensitivity
15   In this section, we discuss the load scenarios and load sensitivity considered in the
16   2025 IRP. This section and Appendix A meet the requirements of part (a) of section
17   44.1(2) of the Utilities Commission Act. This section, supplemented by Appendix A,
18   provides forecasted load scenarios which estimate the demand for electricity
19   BC Hydro would expect to serve if we do not take new demand-side measures
20   during the planning horizon.

21   The BCUC’s Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term resource plan
22   should provide a minimum of two load scenarios which illustrate a reasonable range
23   of potential outcomes. 13 In the 2021 IRP Decision, the BCUC determined that

1    BC Hydro’s use of load scenarios was reasonable, noting its flexibility and the
2    consideration of scenarios collectively, rather than in isolation. 14

3    To account for load uncertainty in the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro has considered three
4    load scenarios:

5    •      May 2025 High Load Forecast Scenario (High Load Scenario);

6    •      May 2025 Reference Load Forecast Scenario (Reference Load Scenario);
7           and

8    •      May 2025 Low Load Forecast Scenario (Low Load Scenario).

9    These scenarios represent a range of possible outcomes with compound annual
10   growth rates for energy from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2050 of 1.8% for the High Load
11   Scenario, 1.4% for the Reference Load Scenario, and 0.5% for the Low Load
12   Scenario. 15 The scenarios reflect varying economic conditions, different paces of
13   electrification, and a range of industrial activity.

14   Each load scenario includes an energy load forecast and a capacity forecast. The
15   energy load forecast is measured in gigawatt hours (GWh) and forecasts the
16   electrical energy needs for each year of our planning horizon. The capacity forecast
17   is measured in megawatts (MW) and considers the peak electricity demand within
18   each year of the planning horizon.

19   We also considered the November 2024 North Coast Large Industrial Load Forecast
20   Sensitivity (North Coast Load Sensitivity) which captures demand potential for
21   mining, liquified natural gas, ports, and other new loads in the North Coast region,
22   above the level of load growth considered for that region in either the Reference or
23   High Load Scenarios. This allows us to examine uncertainties in this region where

1    considerable industrial load growth potential exists alongside transmission supply

3    2.3.1          Load Forecast Uncertainty
4    Forecasting future electricity consumption is inherently uncertain, and recent and
5    ongoing changes in the economic and policy environment introduce further
6    complexity. Sources of uncertainty that could impact future load include:

7    •    Global political and economic changes;

8    •    Global and local changes to climate action policy;

9    •    The timing and scale of potential new large loads, influenced by factors such as
10        global demand, commodity pricing and B.C.’s competitiveness relative to other
11        suppliers.

12   •    Closure or curtailment of existing large industrial customer operations;

13   •    The pace of load growth from electric transportation and space heating; and

14   •    The rate of population and economic growth.

15   2.3.2          Description of Load Scenarios and North Coast Load
16                  Sensitivity
17   The Reference Load Scenario uses well established methods which provide
18   reasonable accuracy over the near term (e.g. five years). The forecast considers
19   historic data, established relationships between load and external variables,
20   economic forecasts, and other information from independent external sources. The
21   Reference Load Scenario includes updates to all key inputs relative to the
22   Updated 2021 IRP and is considered to be more likely than the other load scenarios,
23   over the short to medium term (i.e., five to seven years). However, load forecast




                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                     Page 2-18
                                                                Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    uncertainty increases with time, and over the longer-term BC Hydro does not
2    consider any one load scenario to be more or less likely. 16

3    The High Load Scenario assumes additional large industrial development reflecting
4    economic growth and diversification of trade and faster adoption of light-duty electric
5    vehicles over the near to medium term.

6    The Low Load Scenario assumes a slower pace of electrification, lower industrial
7    and lower economic activity, and stagnant load growth.

8    These load scenarios are presented at a time of economic uncertainty when the
9    Canadian economy is contracting. The Reference and Low Load Scenarios reflect
10   the current economic landscape through considerations such as:

11   •      impacts of shifting trade relationships;

12   •      a slowdown of new vehicle purchases; and

13   •      federal changes to immigration policies resulting in weaker population growth
14          which is expected to have broad impacts across the economy.

15   The Conference Board of Canada says in their BC Regional Economic Outlook
16   2024:

17                “While over a long-time frame it is very likely that a recession
18                will occur, the period of economic contraction (below potential
19                growth) is expected to be offset by an economic rebound (above
20                potential growth) such that the impacts of each of these
21                developments average out to keep economic growth at its
22                potential, on average, over a long timeframe.”

23   The potential for a recession in the near term is contrasted by efforts by the
24   provincial and federal governments to expedite projects to diversify the economy
25   which could grow the economy over the medium to long term. This range of

1    The North Coast Load Sensitivity differs from the load scenarios described above.
2    The load scenarios are developed using our standard load forecast methodology
3    described in Appendix A and aggregates individual customer forecasts into a system
4    level forecast covering the entire BC Hydro integrated system. They include a
5    diverse range of customer types including a large and stable base of residential and
6    commercial customers served at distribution voltages. In contrast, the North Coast
7    Load Sensitivity considers potential new industrial load in the North Coast region
8    over and above what was considered in the Reference or High Load Scenarios. This
9    region has a relatively small residential and commercial customer base, and the
10   majority of potential new load identified in the North Coast Load Sensitivity would be
11   served at transmission voltages with load concentrated in the mining and liquified
12   natural gas industries. The incremental load from the North Coast Load Sensitivity is
13   added to the Reference Load Scenario to produce system level energy and peak
14   demand forecast estimates that can be considered for system planning purposes.

1    The load scenarios are consistent with Bill 31 - the Energy Statutes Amendment Act,
2    2025, tabled by the Government of B.C. on October 20, 2025 that would
3    permanently ban new connections to the BC Hydro electricity grid for cryptocurrency
4    mining and put limits on the power available for data centres, Artificial Intelligence,
5    and hydrogen production for export so that electricity service to these emerging
6    sectors is appropriately prioritized and paced. For example, no new cryptocurrency
7    load is included in the load scenarios and forecasted load for artificial intelligence,
8    data centres, and hydrogen for export are within the announced sector limits. 17

9    In its decision on the Updated 2021 IRP, the BCUC agreed with BC Hydro’s
10   proposed approach to make targeted rather than comprehensive updates to the load
11   scenarios, focusing effort on activities or sectors that have material impact on load
12   (such as the large industrial sector, zero-emission transportation, and changes to the
13   building sector). 18 We used this approach in developing the load scenarios and
14   sensitivity for the 2025 IRP. For example, we were most comprehensive in our
15   development of the Reference Load Scenario, using economic predictors, policy
16   analysis, and historic load data current as of winter 2024 as well as customer by
17   customer assessment of large industrial accounts as of spring 2025. For the North
18   Coast Load Sensitivity, we analyzed the status and outlook for each potential large
19   new load in the North Coast region based on available information as of November
20   2024. However, for the Low Load and High Load Scenarios we focused on targeted
21   updates only. For example, the High and Reference Load Scenarios are similar for
22   Residential and Commercial customers, and the Low Load Scenario relies on some
23   inputs from winter 2023 or spring 2024.

1    Two factors contributing to overall lower load in the 2025 load scenarios relative to
2    2023 load scenarios are:

3    •    The economic outlook has changed; for example, the Conference Board of
4         Canada’s BC Regional Economic Outlook 2024 indicates that slower population
5         gains are set to have broad-based economic impacts.

6    •    A slow down in some segments of the economy such as industrial forestry has
7         been more pronounced than anticipated in 2023.

8    The 2025 High Load Scenario is lower than the 2023 Accelerated Electrification
9    Load Scenario by 5,800 GWh in fiscal 2032 and 4,000 GWh in fiscal 2042 primarily
10   due to:

11   •    Global and local changes to climate action which have impacted load growth.
12        For example, since 2023, the development of global markets for green
13        hydrogen has slowed, reducing the potential for load growth associated with
14        hydrogen production by electrolysis that was reflected in the 2023 Accelerated
15        Electrification Load Scenario.

16   •    The 2023 Accelerated Electrification Scenario represented electricity load
17        impacts associated with the Government of B.C.’s greenhouse gas emission
18        reduction targets in the years 2025, 2030, and 2040. As such, it assumed
19        widespread electrification of building space heating beyond what would be
20        expected under current policy. In the 2025 High and Reference load scenarios,
21        we assume new buildings in municipalities which have adopted Zero Carbon
22        Building Codes use heat pumps for space heating. This increases space
23        heating load relative to the April 2023 Reference Load Forecast but not to the
24        same level as the 2023 Accelerated Electrification Scenario which also included
25        the assumption of extensive electrification of existing building space heating.

26   The 2025 Reference Load Scenario is 2,400 GWh lower than the April 2023
27   Reference Load Forecast in fiscal 2032 and 700 GWh higher in fiscal 2042. In the

1    near term, the revised economic outlook and lower industrial forestry load discussed
2    above result in lower load. Over the longer term these factors are offset by two
3    primary factors which increase load:

4    •      The focus on diversifying trade had increased the outlook for mining, oil and
5           gas (including LNG) relative to the outlook in 2023, although in some cases the
6           timing of large new loads has moved out due to project delays.

7    •      The 2025 Reference Load Scenario includes electrification of building space
8           heating and residential water heating for BC municipalities which have adopted
9           Zero Carbon Building Codes for new construction. This increases space
10          heating load relative to the April 2023 Reference Load Forecast, as mentioned
11          above.

16   increased probabilities for new projects and expansions in the 2025 Low Load
17   Scenario relative to the 2023 Low Load Scenario.

11   2.3.4.2         Cross-price elasticity
12   We interpret cross-price elasticity in this context to refer to the relationship between
13   natural gas prices and electricity demand (i.e. if natural gas prices go up then more
14   customers will choose to use more electricity). BC Hydro does not explicitly model a
15   cross-price elasticity assumption in our load scenarios; however, the costs of
16   competing fuels are considered. For example:

17   •      For large industrial load forecasts, BC Hydro forecasts load on an individual site
18          basis considering the business cases and business plans of our large industrial
19          customers, which consider the cost of competing fuels.

20   •      For residential load forecasts, BC Hydro uses data collected from our
21          Residential End Use Survey to set the base year end use shares. These end
22          use shares reflect customer choices of home heating equipment which are
23          informed by their consideration of fuel costs.

12   2.3.5           Load Forecast Methodology
13   The BCUC Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term resource plan
14   should include an explanation of the methodological approach used for demand
15   forecasting and a summary of the most significant changes to assumptions, inputs or
16   methodologies since the filing of the previous resource plan. 31 The load scenarios
17   presented in the 2025 IRP were developed by BC Hydro using our standard load
18   forecast methodologies which are described in Appendix A. This section
19   summarizes the key methodological changes in the 2025 IRP relative to the Updated
20   2021 IRP.


     31   Sections 2 (b) and 8 (a) of the 2025 Resource Planning Guidelines.



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                Page 2-42
                                                               Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    In their decision on the Updated 2021 IRP, the BCUC encouraged BC Hydro to align
2    load forecast methodologies across all load scenarios to allow for an ‘apples to
3    apples ’comparison of results. The 2025 IRP meets this request, and all forecast
4    scenario outputs can now be presented on a rate class and locational basis. This
5    differs from our Updated 2021 IRP where one scenario used a top-down method in
6    which results could not be disaggregated by rate class or location, while two
7    scenarios used our standard method and could be disaggregated by rate class and
8    location.

9    We also improved our methods and inputs for forecasting electrification loads of
10   space heating and electric vehicles, by incorporating new empirical load research
11   and expanding our modeling capabilities for Zero Carbon Building Codes and
12   electric vehicles. This differs from the demand forecasts used in the
13   Updated 2021 IRP where electric vehicle peak demand was based on load
14   simulation and our standard load forecast method did not have the capability to
15   model and forecast Zero Carbon Building Codes.

16   While the load scenarios include significant fuel switching that avoids or reduces
17   greenhouse gas emissions, no load scenarios are assumed to meet province wide
18   BC GHG emission targets. This differs from our Updated 2021 IRP where one load
19   scenario was assumed to meet the province wide BC GHG emissions target in the
20   years 2025, 2030, and 2040.


21   2.4            Planning Criteria
22   Planning criteria refers to the technical measurement of what constitutes sufficiently
23   reliable energy, capacity and transmission. In the Updated 2021 IRP, there was
24   particular interest expressed in the 1-day-in-10-years Loss of Load Expectation
25   standard (LOLE Standard) 32 which underpins BC Hydro’s capacity planning criteria.


     32   The one-day-in-10-years LOLE standard is our generation capacity planning criterion. It defines an
          adequate generation system as one that has an expectation of being unable to serve the daily peak demand
          less than one day in ten years.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                       Page 2-43
                                                                   Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    The Commission recognized that the LOLE Standard is a well-established industry
2    practice but also recognized the need to consider whether it remains appropriate
3    given the pace of change in B.C.’s energy systems. The LOLE Standard has been in
4    place since the mid-1970s and any changes to it, or other aspects of BC Hydro’s
5    planning criteria, would need to be carefully considered and developed through a
6    multi-step process. As a first step, for the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro has focused on:

7    •      Improving the quality and accuracy of input data;

8    •      Reassessing the capacity contributions of resources; and

9    •      Reviewing the capacity reserve requirement.

10   2.4.1           Generation Energy Planning Criteria
11   BC Hydro’s energy planning criteria defines the amount of electrical energy that can
12   be reliably counted on from our generation system for long-term resource planning.
13   This is referred to as energy capability.

14   Energy capability is based on:

15   •      BC Hydro-owned hydroelectric resources under average water conditions,
16          consistent with the Clean Energy Act and the Electricity Self-Sufficiency
17          Regulation; 33

18   •      IPP-owned hydroelectric resources under contract to BC Hydro through
19          electricity purchase agreements, coinciding with the BC Hydro system critical
20          water conditions; and

21   •      other resource types (e.g., wind, biomass), based on average generation, as
22          their output does not vary with water conditions.

1    Taken together, BC Hydro’s system energy capability is approximately 65,000 GWh

3    critical/dry conditions to about 14,000 GWh more under wet conditions. This
4    variability is managed operationally through reservoir management (drawdowns,

6    2.4.2           Generation Capacity Planning Criterion
7    BC Hydro’s capacity planning criterion defines the amount of generation capacity
8    that can be reliably counted on to meet peak electricity demand consistent with the
9    Clean Energy Act and the Electricity Self-Sufficiency Regulation. This is referred to
10   as peak load carrying capability.

11   We use probabilistic models and various methods to evaluate:

12   •     Capacity contributions of different resources; and

13   •     The capacity reserve needed to meet the LOLE Standard.

14   2.4.2.2          Capacity reserve (R)
15   To meet the LOLE Standard, additional generation capacity is required to account
16   for uncontrollable risks such as equipment failure or fuel shortages. This capacity
17   reserve is calculated using a probabilistic model and expressed as a percentage of




                               BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                  Page 2-46
                                                                  Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    dependable capacity from non-variable generation. 34,35 It represents the difference
2    (in megawatts) between the peak load and the amount of generation capacity
3    needed to serve that peak load while meeting the LOLE Standard.

4    For the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro reassessed the capacity reserve requirement by re-
5    running our probabilistic model with updated input data and associated uncertainties.
6    The updated inputs included load shapes that better reflect demand patterns
7    observed following the COVID-19 pandemic, forced outage rates for BC Hydro’s
8    generating assets based on more recent asset performance, and extended historical
9    generation records to March 2024. This analysis re-affirmed that the 12 percent
10   reserve requirement used in the Updated 2021 IRP remains appropriate to meet the
11   LOLE Standard.

1    The ELCC for run-of-river was unchanged at 15% because more recent generation

3    We focused our efforts on reviewing the ELCC factor for on-shore wind because we
4    expect wind to be the more likely new resource to meet future electricity needs,
5    given its relative cost and availability. For the 2025 IRP, we considered how the
6    ELCC for on-shore wind could change depending on the amount of wind resource
7    additions and the geographic distribution of those additions. The amount of wind
8    resource additions can impact the ELCC because at higher amounts, the extent to
9    which those wind resources can be integrated into BC Hydro’s system declines.
10   Geographic distribution can impact the ELCC because the probability there is some
11   wind projects generating when the electricity is needed is higher when the wind
12   projects are distributed throughout the province, subject to diversified wind regimes,
13   versus if the wind projects are concentrated in a particular region, subject to similar
14   wind regimes.

15   We determined that the ELCC of 24% remains appropriate. The 2024 Call for Power
16   resulted in a relatively broad geographic distribution of wind projects and we expect
17   future calls to have a degree of distribution that will support continuing with this
18   ELCC assumption. To the extent that geographic distribution becomes more
19   concentrated, the ELCC for wind resources could decline. 36

8    2.4.3          Transmission Planning Criteria
9    BC Hydro’s transmission planning criteria define transmission system capability for
10   long-term resource planning. These criteria remain unchanged from the
11   Updated 2021 IRP and are based on:

12   •      North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) TPL-001-4 mandatory
13          reliability standard;

14   •      Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) TPL-001-WECC-CRT-4
15          criterion; and

16   •      BC Hydro’s internal generation dispatch guidelines. 39

17   2.4.4          Resource Adequacy Interest Group
18   In response to the issues raised during the 2021 IRP proceeding, BC Hydro formed
19   the Resource Adequacy Interest Group (RAIG) 40 to review our planning criteria
20   going forward.

21   The RAIG met in June 2024 and discussed the following topics:

22   •      BC Hydro’s resource adequacy methodology;



     39   Refer to Appendix H-3 of the 2021 IRP Application.
     40   The RAIG consists of interveners and members of the IRP Technical Advisory Group who expressed interest
          in participating.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                     Page 2-50
                                                      Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    •    Industry practices and trends in resource adequacy metrics, including
2         approaches to representing capacity contributions (e.g., ELCC, dependable
3         capacity);

4    •    Issues raised during the 2021 IRP proceeding, such as:

5          The appropriateness of the LOLE Standard;

6          Whether capacity reserve should be expressed as a percentage of load or
7            generation;

8          The capacity reserve requirement. Specifically, whether it is too high and
9            should be adjusted so that the cost does not outweigh the risk it is trying to
10           address or whether it is too low and should be adjusted to be more stringent,
11           particularly with regard to regional reliability; and

12         Next steps for reviewing BC Hydro’s planning criteria.

13   Participants expressed that they found the session informative and appreciated the
14   opportunity to provide input and share their perspectives.

15   Based on feedback from the RAIG, BC Hydro has prioritized the following steps to
16   advance work on planning criteria. These efforts will inform future discussions on
17   potential updates to our planning criteria such as the LOLE Standard and the
18   capacity reserve.

19   1.   Evolving Resource Adequacy Modeling – Enhancing input data and
20        modeling capabilities to better reflect changing demand patterns, such as
21        increased electric vehicle adoption, and evolving resource characteristics, in
22        order to identify emerging reliability risks.

23   2.   Exploring Additional Metrics – Assessing alternative ways to represent
24        resource adequacy risk beyond the LOLE Standard. For example, BC Hydro
25        will consider metrics such as expected unserved energy over a season.

1    2.7             Resource Options
2    In this section, we discuss the demand-side and supply-side resource options that
3    are available to meet future electricity needs and were considered as potential
4    planned resources for the 2025 IRP. The BCUC’s Resource Planning Guidelines
5    state that a long-term resource plan should list feasible demand-side and supply-
6    side resource options and outline their main attributes and uncertainties. 52

7    2.7.1           Demand-side Measures Resource Options
8    Demand-side measures are programs and rate structures designed to influence how
9    and when customers use electricity, ultimately aimed at reducing energy
10   consumption or shifting demand to off-peak hours. Demand-side measures have two
11   attractive features for the purposes of resource planning:

12   •      they have lead times of two to three years which are shorter than the lead times
13          for electricity supply resources such as wind and solar; 53 and

14   •      they offer flexibility to ramp up or ramp down in response to a changing load
15          environment.

16   Demand-side measures fall into three categories, which are explained further in the
17   subsections below:

18   •      Energy efficiency;

19   •      Demand Response; and

20   •      Customer Solar.

21   2.7.1.1         Energy Efficiency
22   Energy efficiency programs focus on improving the efficiency of customer electricity
23   use by addressing barriers to cost-effective energy savings through marketing and
24   awareness activities as well as financial incentives for customer studies, projects

     52   Section 3 (a) of the 2025 Resource Planning Guidelines.

4    2.7.1.2          Demand Response
5    Demand response programs enable and incentivize customers to shift their load
6    away from peak demand periods.

7    Programs can include those where BC Hydro directly manages59 the customer’s
8    device during a peak event in exchange for a financial incentive as well as
9    behavioural programs where customers receive an incentive for taking action to
10   reduce load during an event.

11   In the Updated 2021 IRP, demand response programs were combined with time-
12   varying rates, and the capacity savings from demand response programs were
13   estimated using results from the Demand Response Potential Study. 60

14   For the 2025 IRP, demand response programs are considered as a standalone to
15   enable more detailed analysis and independent decision-making going forward.
16   Further, the savings and costs associated with Electric Vehicle Peak Reduction are
17   no longer treated as a distinct resource option. Instead, they have been incorporated
18   into the applicable demand response programs and time-varying rates.

4    2.7.1.3        Customer Solar
5    Customer Solar resource options involve incentives and marketing efforts to support
6    customer adoption of behind-the-meter solar, or solar paired with battery storage.
7    These systems enable customers to reduce the amount of electricity they receive
8    from BC Hydro and may also result in excess generation being delivered to the grid.

9    To develop the Customer Solar resource options for the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro
10   engaged Dunsky Energy + Climate Advisors to assess the potential of these
11   technologies. 66 The assessment examined behind-the-meter solar photovoltaic (PV)
12   systems and solar PV paired with battery storage for residential and general service
13   customers under several scenarios.

14   The assessment estimated the technical potential (i.e., the theoretical maximum
15   adoption) based on building stock, site suitability for solar, and the generation profile
16   of installed systems. Dunsky’s in-house Solar Adoption Model was then used to
17   project solar adoption based on customer economics and technology diffusion
18   theory. 67

1    2.7.2           Distributed Generation Resource Options
2    Distributed generation resources are small-scale generation and storage systems
3    located close to where the energy generated is consumed. These systems may be
4    customer-owned and located behind the customer’s meter, where the generation
5    primarily offsets that customer’s electricity use. Alternatively, they may be directly
6    connected to the BC Hydro grid at distribution voltage, serving load generally in the
7    surrounding area.

8    Although the unit costs of distributed generation resources tend to be higher than
9    those of utility-scale equivalents, they offer several advantages. These include
10   shorter lead times, reduced transmission system losses due to proximity to load
11   centres, and the potential to avoid interconnection and transmission system
12   bottlenecks.

13   2.7.2.1         Customer Solar
14   Customer solar is described in section 2.7.1.3 above.

15   2.7.2.2         Distributed Solar
16   Distributed solar refers to solar systems sized between 1 MW and 15 MW that
17   connect directly to the BC Hydro grid at distribution voltage. 74 For the 2025 IRP, this
18   resource option has been updated with new capital cost information based on
19   indicative project costs for distributed-scale solar projects in 2023. 75

20   BC Hydro’s resource options inventory includes almost 60 distributed solar resource
21   options, totalling 630 GWh per year of potential generation. The Unit Energy Cost for
22   distributed solar resources brought into service in fiscal 2034 ranges from $87 to
23   over $400 per MWh.

          Technology Investment Tax Credit as described in section 2.7.3.

1    2.7.2.3         Distributed Batteries
2    Distributed batteries consist of a small number of battery modules that can be
3    deployed close to, or within, existing distribution substations. 76 For the 2025 IRP,
4    this resource option has been updated with new capital cost information based on
5    indicative project costs provided by a consultant, working with BC Hydro on battery
6    pilots and programs. 77 The indicative project costs are for 15 MW and 60 MWh
7    lithium-ion battery systems that would be located in British Columbia.

8    BC Hydro’s resource options inventory for distributed batteries includes 250 MW of
9    installed capacity, with an estimated cost of $200 per kW-year for installations
10   completed in fiscal 2034.

11   Battery systems are expected to play an important though limited role in providing
12   system capacity going forward. Batteries offer flexibility in terms of siting and
13   operation and can provide additional utility value streams, such as voltage support,
14   frequency regulation and emergency back up, particularly when located at strategic
15   points on the distribution system. However, they are constrained to approximately
16   four hours of maximum generation before recharging is required.

17   2.7.3           Supply Resource Options – Intermittent Energy
18   This section describes utility-scale, supply-side generation resource options that
19   provide intermittent energy – including onshore wind, offshore wind, utility-scale
20   solar, and run-of-river hydro resources. Intermittent resources cannot be scheduled
21   and do not contribute dependable capacity to the grid. However, they do contribute
22   to the Effective Load Carrying Capability of the BC Hydro system, to the extent that
23   their winter generation profiles align with the system’s winter load needs.

24   These resource options are larger than their distributed-scale counterparts and
25   connect to the BC Hydro grid at transmission voltage. They benefit from economies

1    2.7.3.1         Onshore Wind
2    There are onshore wind energy resource options throughout British Columbia. 79 For
3    the 2025 IRP, the onshore wind resource inventory has been updated to reflect the
4    following:

5    •      Removal of 10 potential projects in the Peace Region due to regulatory
6           changes aimed at permanently enhancing caribou protection;

7    •      Reduction of maximum capacity factors for resources in the Peace Region. This
8           is because input from stakeholders involved in BC Hydro’s 2024 Call for Power
9           suggested that the quality of wind resources in the Peace region is lower than
10          indicated by BC Hydro’s wind modelling. Based on this feedback, capacity
11          factors for Peace Region wind resources were reduced to a maximum of 43%;
12          and

13   •      Updates to project costs based on a literature review to capture the real (as
14          opposed to nominal) capital cost increases between 2021 to 2023. These
15          updates were generally validated through comparison with bids received during
16          the 2024 Call for Power process.

17   BC Hydro compared the cost, performance and lead time characteristics of onshore
18   wind resource options against the aggregate cost and performance characteristics of
19   winning bidders from the 2024 Call for Power. In general, the average capital costs
20   of the portfolio of projects awarded electricity purchase agreements were within the
21   higher end of the estimated cost range and the quality of potential wind output varies
22   by region.

23   In total, BC Hydro’s resource options inventory for onshore wind includes more than
24   110 projects, representing approximately 44,000 GWh per year of potential
25   generation, with estimated lead times of five to eight years.

10   updated based on a literature review to reflect real capital cost increases from 2021
11   to 2023. These updates were validated through industry engagement and
12   comparison with solar bids submitted during BC Hydro’s 2024 Call for Power.

13   BC Hydro’s resource options inventory for utility-scale solar includes 190 potential
14   sites, with a combined generation potential of nearly 24,000 GWh per year and lead
15   times ranging from five to eight years.

16   Although utility-scale solar is currently more expensive on a per-MWh basis than
17   onshore wind, the cost difference is relatively small and expected to decline over
18   time. While capital costs for both wind and solar are projected to decrease, solar
19   costs are expected to fall more rapidly due to continued improvements in solar panel
20   efficiency, manufacturing processes, and supply chain optimization. In BC Hydro’s
21   context, utility-scale solar and onshore wind resources may reach cost parity in the
22   late 2030s or early 2040s.

4    2.7.5.1    Pumped Storage Hydro
5    For the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro has updated the inventory of pumped storage hydro
6    resource options by distinguishing between long-duration and short-duration
7    systems.

8    Long-duration pumped storage is defined as having sufficient storage volume to
9    generate at maximum output during all peak load hours of a typical winter cold snap,
10   providing an ELCC value approaching 100%. A desktop study conducted by Kerr
11   Wood Leidal Associates and Lombardi Consultants identified and characterized a
12   shortlist of viable long duration pumped storage options. BC Hydro applied their
13   methodology to update the cost and performance of suitable options already in our
14   resource options inventory. The updated inventory includes 31 long-duration
15   pumped storage hydro resource options capable of providing more than 10 GW of
16   capacity, with lead times of approximately 10 years.

17   Short duration pumped storage systems provide approximately 6 hours of daily
18   generation and have ELCC values between 5 and 50%. These resources were not
19   updated for the 2025 IRP due to the absence of significant technological or market
20   changes for this mature technology since the Updated 2021 IRP.

8   2025 IRP. The BCUC’s Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term

5    BC Hydro consulted on the 2025 IRP through three streams: a First Nations stream,
6    a public stream, and a technical stream consisting of a Technical Advisory
7    Committee.

8    The First Nations and public streams each occurred in two phases: Phase 1
9    occurred from May 2024 to September 2024, gathering broad input as the 2025 IRP
10   was being developed. Phase 2 occurred through June to August 2025, gathering
11   feedback on the plan elements for the 2025 IRP. Feedback was also gathered from
12   the Technical Advisory Committee on planning inputs and analysis, including the
13   load scenarios, approach to managing uncertainty, along with the plan elements and
14   Near-term Actions.

15   Further information, including our consultation activities and materials for the three
16   streams, is available at bchydro.com/2025irp. Phase 1 consultation and engagement
17   is discussed below. Phase 2 consultation and engagement is discussed in Section 3.

18   2.8.1           First Nations stream
19   BC Hydro, as a Crown corporation, must act honourably in its dealings with First
20   Nations, which includes the consideration of First Nations’ rights and interests in the
21   context of long-term resource planning. The duty to consult, grounded in the honour




     94   Section 6 (a) of the 2025 Resource Planning Guidelines.



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                               Page 2-80
                                                                     Planning Context and Decision Framework




1    of the Crown, protects the rights recognized and affirmed in section 35 of the
2    Constitution Act, 1982 and aims to advance the process of reconciliation. 95,96

3    The Supreme Court of Canada has established key principles in Haida, and the
4    cases following it that continue to guide the Crown in fulfilling its duty to consult. 97
5    These principles include that the scope of consultation required will fall on a
6    “spectrum”98 ranging from “low” to “moderate” to “deep” consultation depending on
7    the specific context, and will be proportionate to a preliminary assessment of the
8    strength of claim supporting the existence of the right or title, and seriousness of the
9    potential adverse impact upon the right or title, asserted. 99

10   BC Hydro recognizes that the duty to consult extends to “strategic, higher-level
11   decisions” that may have an impact on Aboriginal claims and rights. 100

12   The development of the 2025 IRP is consistent with the nature of a strategic
13   planning decision with very low potential to create adverse impacts, if any, on
14   Aboriginal rights and title. 101 This is because the 2025 IRP is a plan dependent on
15   future customer need for electricity and other factors that are subject to change and
16   any projects contemplated by the 2025 IRP will be subject to separate consultation
17   and approval processes before proceeding. These separate processes will provide



     95    The underlying purpose of section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 is to achieve “the reconciliation of
           Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Canadians in a mutually respectful long-term relationship." (Beckman v. Little
           Salmon/Carmacks First Nation, 2010 SCC 53, at para. 10.)
     96    The 2010 First Nations Information Filing Guidelines for Crown Utilities set out information needed to
           facilitate and enable the BCUC to assess whether the Crown’s duty to consult and, if necessary,
           accommodate First Nations is fulfilled prior to the BCUC’s decision. While BC Hydro has considered these
           guidelines with respect to the information filed in support of this application from a consultation perspective,
           BC Hydro has also been guided by the legal requirements and the BCUC’s expectations as they have
           evolved since 2010.

     98    Haida, at paras. 43-45.
