3    2.8.1.2           Themes emerging during Phase 1: Gathering input into the plan
4    The following key themes arising from Phase 1 informed the development of the
5    2025 IRP:

6    •        Participants had a keen interest in clean energy opportunities, including
7             project ownership for First Nations: First Nations have expressed strong
8             interest in ownership and economic benefits from projects arising from IRP
9             Near-term Actions, particularly in clean energy initiatives in response to calls for
10            power.



                                BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                           Page 2-83
                                                   Planning Context and Decision Framework




1         The 2025 IRP includes a new energy acquisition process as a Near-term
2           Action, and First Nations project ownership will be part of the
3           implementation of this Near-term Action.

4    •   Participants expressed concerns about the environment and the importance
5        of minimizing further impacts on land and water resources: Participants
6        recommended that BC Hydro prioritize upgrading existing infrastructure,
7        increase capacity at current facilities, align with First Nations’ stewardship
8        plans, and encourage energy conservation over new development.

9         The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by continuing to focus on demand-side
10          measures and by advancing upgrades to existing generation facilities.

11   •   Participants stressed the importance of energy conservation and
12       affordability: There was broad support for energy efficiency and conservation
13       programs, particularly if participation is voluntary. Participants shared the
14       importance of balancing new generation with expanding conservation
15       programs.

16        The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by continuing to focus on demand-side
17          measures, including the addition of a customer solar program.

18   •   Participants expressed interest in exploring different types of technologies.
19       There was interest in diverse technologies (like tidal and batteries) for future
20       calls for power and as a potential method to improve reliability in remote, end-
21       of-line communities.

22        The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by preparing for utility-scale batteries
23          and exploring future capacity resources through a Capacity Request for
24          Expression of Interest.

25   •   Participants expressed concern about climate change and a desire for it to be
26       addressed in long-term resource planning. Participants expressed that climate




                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                    Page 2-84
                                                                  Planning Context and Decision Framework




1            impacts should be mitigated and decisions that have long-term implications for
2            the climate should be made in collaboration with First Nations.

3             The 2025 IRP identifies planned resources and Near-term Actions to meet
4                the demand associated with customer electrification decisions, helping to
5                reduce greenhouse gases in support of climate action (e.g., advancing the
6                2025 Call for Power for clean or renewable resources, advancing upgrades
7                to facilities, exploring new technologies, and advancing a customer solar
8                program).

9    Consultation on the 2025 IRP is BC Hydro’s first step in engaging First Nations with
10   respect to plans to meet future energy needs and which projects may be pursued to
11   meet these needs. Consultation will continue as we implement the 2025 IRP and
12   move forward with projects or plans which may impact Aboriginal title or rights.
13   Given BC Hydro’s level of consultation, the incorporation of First Nations’ input into
14   the development of the 2025 IRP, and the nature of First Nations’ feedback on the
15   2025 IRP, BC Hydro submits that it has met or exceeded its legal obligation to
16   consult.

3   2.8.2.2              Themes emerging during Phase 1: Gathering input into the plan
4   The following key themes arising from Phase 1 informed the development of the
5   2025 IRP.

6   •        Participants placed a high priority on keeping costs down when asked
7            about planning objectives, with cost-of-living concerns being top of mind.
8            Survey respondents ranked keeping costs down as highest priority, followed by
9            reducing provincial greenhouse gas emissions through clean electricity.


                                BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                          Page 2-86
                                                   Planning Context and Decision Framework




1        Responses were mixed about when to spend on resources – some participants
2        said to wait until BC Hydro is more certain of demand while others preferred
3        being proactive to support economic growth and climate action, even if it meant
4        paying a bit more on their bills.

5         The 2025 IRP is proactive by advancing new resources to support economic
6           growth and climate action but also considers ways to keep costs down by
7           maintaining flexibility through demand-side measures that can be ramped
8           down if needed and planning to undertake more frequent IRPs so that
9           BC Hydro can adjust as conditions change.

10   •   Participants support conservation and energy management initiatives,
11       including distributed generation. Energy efficiency and demand response
12       programs were both well supported by participants. Respondents preferred
13       balancing generation resource development and scaling up of energy efficiency
14       programs. Participants also expressed interest in more localized solutions for
15       energy and capacity resources, such as community and residential solar.

16        The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by continuing with conservation and
17          energy management initiatives, including a new customer solar program,
18          which enables more distributed resource development. It also continues with
19          a mix of conservation and energy management initiatives and generation
20          resource development.

21   •   Participants support a diverse mix of renewable power generation (e.g.
22       wind, solar, and other options) in efforts to mitigate climate change impacts.

23        The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by advancing the 2025 Call for Power for
24          clean or renewable resources which will help to meet the energy
25          consumption associated with customer electrification decisions.

26   •   Participants were mixed regarding preferred clean or renewable capacity
27       additions with many having no strong preference. Survey respondents were
28       mixed regarding preferences for pumped storage and battery storage options.


                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                  Page 2-87
                                                                 Planning Context and Decision Framework




1            Many participants choosing pumped storage considered this resource to have
2            comparatively less environmental impacts, while participants choosing batteries
3            considered this resource to be portable and easily deployable. Many
4            respondents expressed no strong preference among the capacity options
5            presented.

6             The 2025 IRP aligns with this input by moving forward with upgrades to
7                existing facilities which are the lowest environmental impact capacity
8                resource options and advancing a Capacity Request for Expressions of
9                Interest to consider future capacity resource options.

10   2.8.3           Technical Stream
11   BC Hydro established the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) to provide ongoing
12   advice and feedback through the development of the 2025 IRP.

13   The TAC members represented diverse interests, such as customer groups, First
14   Nations, environmental, independent power producers, sustainable energy,
15   municipal government, low income, and other utilities.

16   The TAC met five times between May 2024 and July 2025 for discussions on
17   planning assumptions, inputs and analysis, implementation of UNDRIP, and to
18   provide feedback on the elements of the 2025 IRP. 105

19   The TAC Engagement Report is provided in Appendix E. It includes the Terms of
20   Reference, membership, process details, and a summary of feedback and how it
21   was considered in the 2025 IRP.

7   •   Keeping costs down for customers;

13   2.9.3            Considering Uncertainty in the 2025 IRP
14   As discussed in section 2.2 above, geopolitical instability and shifting trade
15   relationships, changing economic conditions, technological advancements and
16   climate variability are all contributing to uncertain load and supply outlooks.
17   BC Hydro considers the uncertainty associated with these factors to be material.
18   Accordingly, the consideration of uncertainty is an important focus of this
19   2025 IRP. 112

20   BC Hydro identified the following uncertainties as the most impactful for the
21   2025 IRP:

1    3.1            Introduction
2    This Chapter sets out BC Hydro’s 2025 IRP.

3    In accordance with section 44.1(2) of the Utilities Commission Act, the 2025 IRP
4    starts by considering demand-side measures (DSM) to meet energy and capacity
5    needs. 1 Once the levels of DSM have been selected, it considers the supply-side
6    energy and capacity resources to meet remaining needs as well as transmission
7    resources to meet capacity needs in the three transmission constrained regions –
8    South Coast, Vancouver Island and North Coast. All of these decisions are informed
9    by feedback received through consultation and engagement.

10   The 2025 IRP continues with the flexible approach to resource planning adopted for
11   the Updated 2021 IRP, which was endorsed by the BCUC in its decision. 2 It
12   considers the uncertainty outlined in Chapter 2 and focuses on being ready for many
13   potential futures, emphasizing ranges rather than static targets for various plan
14   elements to increase flexibility to respond to changing circumstances.

15   As set out below, key features of the 2025 IRP include plans to:

16   •     Pursue higher levels of demand-side measures than in the Updated 2021 IRP,
17         such as Energy Efficiency Program B and Customer Solar A, which provide
18         greater flexibility to respond to various external factors that could cause the
19         load to be higher or lower;

20   •     Acquire up to 5,000 GWh of new energy resources by fiscal 2034, and
21         preparing to acquire or build additional clean or renewable energy resources
22         should further need arise; and



     1   Section 44.1 of the UCA sets out the requirements for a long-term resource plan. The UCA and Clean
         Energy Acy indicate a clear policy preference for the priority use of cost-effective demand-side measures.
         The consultation feedback we received as we developed the Updated 2021 IRP and the 2025 IRP is
         consistent with this priority.
     2   2021 IRP Decision (pps. 25, 32, 41) and Order (p. 11).



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                            Page 3-1
                                                                               2025 Integrated Resource Plan




1    •     Build two significant BC Hydro system expansions to meet future capacity
2          needs: a sixth generating unit at Revelstoke Generating Station and a second
3          transmission line to the North Coast.

4    The elements of the 2025 IRP and their associated Near-term Actions all utilize
5    clean or renewable energy and therefore advance the recently modified energy
6    objective 2(c) of the Clean Energy Act. 3


7    3.2            Demand-Side Measures (Section 44.1(2) of the UCA
8                   Parts B, C and F)
9    This section of the 2025 IRP meets the requirements of parts (b), (c) and (f) of
10   section 44.1(2) of the Utilities Commission Act. It sets out BC Hydro’s plan of how
11   we intend to reduce demand by taking cost-effective demand-side measures and
12   provides an estimate of the remaining energy demand after these measures are
13   implemented. It also explains why the new supply that we plan to acquire is not
14   planned to be replaced by demand-side measures.

15   Compared to the Updated 2021 IRP, the 2025 IRP pursues higher levels of demand-
16   side measures. We have selected a higher level of energy efficiency, Energy
17   Efficiency Programs B, and have added a new element: Customer Solar A.

18   A higher level of energy efficiency supports flexibility, which is an important feature
19   of the 2025 IRP due to the various external factors that could cause load to be
20   higher or lower over both the short and longer term. Higher energy efficiency
21   supports flexibility because it has shorter lead times and can be ramped down or
22   accelerated in response to updated forecast needs.

23   The following sub-sections discuss the analysis and selection of the plan elements
24   Energy Efficiency Programs B and Customer Solar A for the 2025 IRP. The BCUC’s

5    Programs A has cost and cost-risk advantages over Energy Efficiency Programs B
6    under the Reference Load Scenario, it has higher land and water impacts and also

14   On this basis, BC Hydro selected Energy Efficiency Programs B. A higher level of
15   energy efficiency supports flexibility. If need is lower, measures can be ramped
16   down quickly to capture some of the cost advantages of Energy Efficiency
17   Programs A. If need is higher, Energy Efficiency Programs B has relatively short
18   lead times to respond and can be accelerated, with comparable cost impacts to

     8       For more information, please see Appendix H where we discuss the uncertainty of how wind projects added

                                           BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                                                                         Page 3-5

1    supply-side resources. This flexibility to respond is an important feature due to the
2    various external factors that could cause load to be higher or lower over both the
3    short and longer term.

4    Staying the course with Energy Efficiency Programs A would not have provided the
5    same type of flexibility. This is because it would take more time to ramp up to higher
6    levels of energy efficiency compared to the amount of time required to ramp down if
7    need is lower. Ramping up can involve designing and initiating new programs,
8    recruiting and training additional staff and designing and initiating new information
9    technology systems. It can also involve getting a large network of companies that
10   provide energy efficiency goods and services to BC customers to expand their
11   operations, staffing and stocking practices to support a higher level of program
12   activity. In contrast, ramping down can involve restricting or cancelling programs and
13   workforce management. While these steps may be disruptive, they can be
14   implemented faster than the steps required to ramp up.

5    3.2.4           Consultation feedback and consideration
6    Consultation occurred in two phases. Phase 1 gathered input on IRP planning
7    topics, including demand-side measures, while Phase 2 sought feedback on the
8    selected demand-side measures elements, highlighting the decision to select
9    Customer Solar A. Results from our consultation showed: 12

10   •      In Phase 1 (Input), First Nations and the public were supportive of demand-side
11          measures as a resource option.

12   •      In Phase 2 (Feedback), both the public and First Nations survey respondents13
13          as well as First Nation sessions and one-on-one meeting participants,
14          supported the selected demand-side measures element and the plan to
15          advance a customer solar program citing reasons such as it is clean,
16          renewable, affordable, good for the environment, and a step towards energy
17          independence for First Nations.

9         capacity resources increase;

10   •    Prepare to increase the availability of capacity resource options;

11   •    Prepare to initiate the second step of transmission upgrades to the South Coast
12        and Capacity Upgrades to supply Vancouver Island; and

13   •    Build a second transmission line to the North Coast.

14   The following sub-sections discuss the analysis and selection of these plan
15   elements.

16   3.3.1       2025 IRP Element 4: New Energy Acquisitions
17   As part of the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro will seek to acquire up to 5,000 GWh of energy
18   by fiscal 2034 through a new call for power and other acquisitions. BC Hydro will
19   also prepare to acquire and/or build additional new energy resources to meet longer-
20   term needs.

21   The target of up to 5,000 GWh considers and balances the need to be prepared for
22   load uncertainty and supply uncertainty with the cost risk of any resulting energy
23   surplus.

1    In Table 3-5 above, after the selected demand-side measures 16, the remaining
2    energy deficit in fiscal 2035 ranges from approximately 800 GWh under the
3    Reference Load scenario to approximately 8,300 GWh under the High Load
4    scenario. By fiscal 2040, this increases to a deficit of approximately 3,200 GWh
5    under the Reference Load scenario to approximately 11,200 GWh under the High
6    Load scenario.

7    While load uncertainty is the largest source of uncertainty, resources to meet
8    demand are subject to their own uncertainties. Specifically, initiated resources such
9    as DSM, EPA renewals or EPAs from the 2024 Call for Power may under-deliver or
10   deliver energy later than expected. BC Hydro expects the lead-time for new wind
11   and utility-scale solar resources to be approximately 6 years. However, actual lead
12   times could be shorter or longer. For example, the earliest guaranteed commercial
13   operation date under the 2024 Call for Power is in fiscal 2031, approximately 6 years
14   after the 2024 Call for Power was issued in fiscal 2025; however, some volume is
15   currently expected to be available as early as fiscal 2029, while other projects are
16   not currently expected to supply energy until fiscal 2033. BC Hydro, and the
17   provincial and federal governments are all taking steps to reduce permitting
18   timelines for projects to help to mitigate this uncertainty, but this risk still needs to be
19   considered, and addressed, through long-term resource planning decisions.

20   Planned resources in the 2025 IRP, such as the selected demand-side measures,
21   could also under-perform. In addition, for future energy acquisitions, there is
22   uncertainty regarding whether projects will reach commercial operation, the lead
23   times for projects to reach commercial operation and then, for projects that do reach

1    the risk of being in deficit and unable to meet customers’ demand for energy to be
2    asymmetric. The potential consequences of being short, which range from non-
3    discretionary electricity imports to a dampening effect on economic development and
4    electrification progress to not being able to serve customer load are greater than the
5    time-limited cost impacts of purchasing energy sooner than it may ultimately be
6    required. In addition, the cost impacts of being in surplus can be mitigated, if
7    needed, by measures such as quickly ramping down the flexible demand-side
8    measures selected as part of the 2025 IRP.

9    3.3.1.1     Target Volume of New Energy Acquisitions
10   We considered four levels of new energy acquisitions:

11   •    2,000 GWh;

12   •    3,500 GWh;

13   •    5,000 GWh; and

14   •    6,500 GWh.

15   BC Hydro considers a target volume of 2,000 GWh to be the minimum necessary for
16   a successful competitive call and the approximate energy acquisition volume needed
17   in the 2025 IRP to be able to meet the Reference Load scenario. This volume
18   equates to approximately 4 wind projects, each with an installed capacity of
19   150 MW. In BC Hydro’s view, acquisition targets below this amount risk attracting
20   insufficient bids to achieve competitive results. At the other end of this range, new
21   energy acquisitions of approximately 6,500 GWh represent the volume needed to
22   meet the High Load scenario.

1    As discussed above, BC Hydro considers the risk of being in surplus and the risk of
2    being in deficit to be asymmetric. In BC Hydro’s view, the risks of being short on
3    energy and stifling public policy and government efforts to promote economic
4    growth, diversification, and nation-building infrastructure initiatives, in response to
5    shifting trade relationships and geopolitical uncertainty, are significant.

6    Considering the range of potential future electricity needs and the consequences of
7    not acquiring enough energy for economic development and diversification efforts,
8    BC Hydro selected an energy acquisition target of 5,000 GWh for the 2025 IRP.

9    In BC Hydro’s view, an incremental rate impact of approximately 1.5% by
10   fiscal 2040, which would occur if the Reference Load scenario unfolds and BC Hydro
11   acquires 5,000 GWh of energy in response to the 2025 IRP, is a reasonable
12   potential cost risk to assume in order to be ready to meet the need under the High
13   Load Scenario. The potential of a 1.5% incremental rate impact by fiscal 2040, which
14   could be reduced through adjustments to selected demand-side measures, if
15   needed, is a prudent hedge against the potential consequences to the system, our
16   customers and the province, of being unable to meet potential future need.

17   Table 3-7 above also illustrates that there would be an energy deficit of 3,300 GWh
18   in fiscal 2035 under the High Load Scenario even after acquiring 5,000 GWh of
19   energy. In order to be in a position to meet such future needs if they unfold,
20   BC Hydro will prepare to acquire and/or build additional clean or renewable energy
21   resources beyond the energy acquisition target in this 2025 IRP. The volume and
22   timing will be informed by subsequent load resource balance updates.

1    Vancouver Island. This will allow BC Hydro to proceed with these system upgrades
2    in time should the need arise and if they are determined to be the most cost-effective
3    means of meeting need after considering local supply alternatives.

4    The North Coast region is an economically important region of the province, with
5    existing and proposed mining, liquefied natural gas, and port developments.
6    Currently, the primary source of supply to the region is a single 500 kV transmission
7    line from Prince George to Terrace and there is limited dependable generation within
8    the region.

9    As shown in Table 3-14 above, the remaining regional capacity need for the North
10   Coast is up to 700 MW by fiscal 2038. To meet this need, BC Hydro will pursue the
11   construction of a second transmission line to the North Coast. There are no viable
12   alternatives to a second transmission line. Large-scale clean or renewable
13   dependable capacity resources in the region cannot, on their own, reliably serve
14   large industrial loads that operate at a high load factor.

15   This second transmission line will run parallel to the existing 500 kV line from Prince
16   George to Terrace. It will enable industrial and related development in the northwest,
17   supporting the diversification of British Columbia’s economy and trade relationships.
18   BC Hydro will work with the Government of B.C. and affected First Nations to consult
19   and engage on the new transmission line project and pursue innovative partnership
20   approaches to project development, including an equity opportunity for First Nations
21   to have an option to co-own the new transmission line with BC Hydro.

22   BC Hydro did not construct a consequence table for the North Coast supply given
23   there are no viable alternatives 30 to a second 500 kV transmission line.

24   The BCUC’s Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term resource plan
25   should discuss any significant potential distribution system level impacts associated



     30   Based on current energy objectives in Part 1 of the Clean Energy Act

                                                                                                     Page 3-25

1    with different load scenarios. 31 The non-bulk transmission and distribution system
2    requirements are dependent upon the specific sub-regions in which load growth
3    occurs. These loads can occur in areas at a level as granular as a neighbourhood
4    within which a high-density residential development is taking place, modifying the
5    requirements of the distribution substations and feeders providing service to the
6    neighbourhood. Similarly, the transmission reinforcements required to accommodate
7    new renewable resources will depend upon the specific project selected as part of
8    an acquisition process. In general, resource portfolios that include demand-side
9    measures that provide capacity will likely result in fewer upgrades or additions at the
10   non-bulk and distribution system level. BC Hydro has recognized this benefit in our
11   transmission and distribution marginal cost analysis described in Appendix F.

6    3.4.1           Resiliency Risks
7    The BCUC’s Resource Planning Guidelines state that a long-term resource plan
8    should summarize any significant resiliency risks which may impact the ability to
9    serve forecasted demand and outline potential resource strategies to address these
10   risks. 34

11   Resilience is a broad concept that includes the ability to anticipate, absorb, adapt to
12   and/or rapidly recover from disruptive events. This includes being set up to manage
13   through challenges, incorporating lessons learned into our business processes and
14   preventing disruptions to electricity service.

15   Long-term planning for a reliable and resilient power system is undertaken at two
16   different planning levels within BC Hydro:

17   •      At the long-term resource planning level, through integrated resource plans;
18          and

19   •      At the asset planning level, through capital and maintenance strategies and
20          plans.

21   In an integrated resource plan, BC Hydro’s planning for resiliency focuses on the
22   ability to anticipate, absorb, and recover quickly from unexpected changes in
23   electricity demand, supply, or both. Resiliency is addressed in two key ways:




     34   Section 3 (h) of the 2025 Resource Planning Guidelines.



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                         Page 3-27
                                                                2025 Integrated Resource Plan




1    1.   Flexibility through Near-term Actions: we anticipate uncertainties and
2         incorporate flexibility into integrated resource plans by identifying Near-term
3         Actions that can accommodate a wide range of potential future demand and
4         supply scenarios. We also take the approach of “living” long-term resource plan
5         with frequent updates to manage the uncertainties in BC Hydro’s planning
6         environment. The uncertainties and potential disruptive events, along with
7         resource strategies to address them, are discussed in Appendix H;

8    2.   Reliability through Planning Criteria: we ensure system reliability by
9         developing resource plans that meet our planning criteria, as outlined in section
10        2.4 above. These criteria reflect industry standards and take into account the
11        variability of demand and supply.

12   In addition, this 2025 IRP takes the following specific steps to build a more resilient
13   power system:

14   •    Diversifying resource types: Implementing demand-side measures and
15        issuing calls for power – where wind and solar are expected to be the
16        predominant resource types – alongside our hydro-dominant system. This
17        diversification helps reduce risks associated with dependence on a single
18        resource type, such as hydro during drought conditions.

19   •    Locating resources closer to demand: Customer-based solar programs at or
20        near customer sites can under certain circumstances help mitigate customer
21        impacts related to transmission system outages or localized disruptions.

22   •    Enhancing generation ramping capability: Electricity systems require the
23        ability to ramp generation up and down to match time-varying electricity
24        demand. As more variable generation is integrated, the variability in net load
25        (load less variable generation) increases. Flexible capacity that can respond
26        within minutes becomes increasingly valuable in such a scenario. The
27        construction of Revelstoke 6, preparing to construct G.M. Shrum Units 1 to 5




                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                    Page 3-28
                                                                2025 Integrated Resource Plan




1          and preparing to deploy utility-scale batteries will enhance the system’s
2          ramping capability.

3    3.4.2       Approvals under the Open Access Transmission Tariff
4    Section 8.3.3 of the Updated 2021 IRP provided a description of the Open Access
5    Transmission Tariff (OATT) and explained that BC Hydro, as a Network Integration
6    Transmission Service customer under the OATT, may include high load forecast
7    scenarios and the associated resource plans in its request for Network Integration
8    Transmission Service, if approved by the Commission to do so. The BCUC
9    approved this approach in section 3.6.1 of the 2021 IRP decision, recognizing the
10   need for flexibility in resource planning to address uncertainties in load forecasts and
11   that there are minimal impacts upon third party transmission customers and
12   BC Hydro’s transmission revenue. The BCUC made the following determination
13   regarding the approach: “the approval will allow BC Hydro to proactively study the
14   potential future need for upgrades of the transmission system. In a time of
15   uncertainty, and for long lead time resources such as transmission assets, we
16   believe this is an important mechanism for BC Hydro to ensure we are prepared to
17   respond to a range of future scenarios.”

18   BC Hydro seeks an order approving the Contingency Resource Plans of the
19   2025 IRP for inclusion in a Network Integration Transmission Service update under
20   BC Hydro’s Open Access Transmission Tariff. As was the case with the similar
21   request in the Updated 2021 IRP, this approval will allow BC Hydro to proactively
22   study the potential future need for upgrades of the transmission system and ensure
23   it is prepared to respond to range of future scenarios without material impacts upon
24   third party transmission customers and BC Hydro’s transmission revenue.

1    1           Load Forecast Methodology
2    The load scenarios presented in the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) were
3    developed by BC Hydro using our standard load forecast methodologies described
4    below.

5    1.1         Energy Load Forecast Methodology
6    The energy load forecast, measured in gigawatt hours (GWh), forecasts the total
7    sales, or requirements, for electric energy in a given year. The system energy load
8    forecast is an aggregation of separate forecasts as shown in Figure A-1 below.

9                     Figure A-1     Energy Load Forecast Methodology




10   In addition to the major components above, load additions are made to account for
11   codes and standards overlap, fuel switching, and line losses. The major components
12   of the energy forecast are developed as follows.

13   1.1.1       Residential
14   The residential load forecast considers the forecasted number of residential
15   accounts multiplied by the average use per account plus the portion of light-duty
16   electric vehicle load forecast that is assumed to charge at residential dwellings.




                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 1
                                                                                  Appendix A
                                                           Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    The residential accounts forecast uses regression models considering accounts
2    growth and economic predictors such as housing stock growth rates, employment,
3    and disposable income.

4    To forecast the average use per account, BC Hydro uses industry standard
5    Statistically Adjusted End-Use (SAE) models. The SAE models are calibrated using
6    10 years of historical data and consider the following key variables:

7    •    Real personal disposable income;

8    •    Household size;

9    •    End-use efficiencies;

10   •    End-use shares; and

11   •    Temperature.

12   BC Hydro analyzed the impact of zero carbon building codes adopted by British
13   Columbia (B.C.) municipalities and modeled this effect using our standard SAE
14   energy load forecast methodology. This significant methodological advancement
15   allows BC Hydro to analyze the potential impact of space heating electrification
16   using a consistent methodology. Therefore, in the Reference and High Load
17   Scenarios, the average use per account assumes that new residential dwellings in
18   municipalities which have adopted bylaws intended to reduce greenhouse gas
19   emissions from new buildings will primarily use electric heat pumps for space
20   heating and cooling, and electricity for water heating and cooking.

21   1.1.2       Commercial
22   To forecast commercial load, BC Hydro uses industry standard SAE models. The
23   key variables considered are:

24   •    Employment;

25   •    Retail sales;


                          BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                        Page 2
                                                                                 Appendix A
                                                          Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    •    Commercial output;

2    •    End use efficiencies;

3    •    End use shares; and

4    •    Temperature.

5    The Reference and High Load Scenarios assume that new commercial buildings in
6    municipalities which have adopted bylaws intended to reduce greenhouse gas
7    emissions from new buildings will primarily use electric technology for heating and
8    cooling.

9    The commercial forecast includes the portion of light-duty electric vehicle charging
10   load to occur at public charging spots, workplaces, and parkades in multi-unit
11   residential buildings as well as electric bus charging assumed to occur at distribution
12   voltage.

13   1.1.3       Light Industrial
14   The light industrial forecast methodology for the Reference and High Load Scenarios
15   uses a regression model considering the relationship between light industrial
16   electricity consumption, softwood lumber production, and construction output.

17   The Low Load Scenario uses a regression model considering the relationship
18   between light industrial electricity consumption, housing starts, and primary output
19   (industrial output from production of raw materials).

20   1.1.4       Large Industrial
21   The large industrial forecast is developed on an account-by-account basis,
22   considering information from:

23   •    Industry experts and external consultant production forecasts, facility, and
24        sector-specific market assessments;




                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                         Page 3
                                                                                   Appendix A
                                                            Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    •    Market research and industry analyses by media as well as through
2         subscriptions such as from Wood Mackenzie and Bloomberg;

3    •    Publicly available documents from government agencies such as through
4         environmental assessment certificate processes;

5    •    Publicly available press releases, plans and reports issued by existing
6         customers and by proponents of new industrial facilities; and

7    •    Customer-specific information gathered by our Key Account Management,
8         Business and Economic Development, and Load Interconnections groups, who
9         are in contact with our customers and with proponents of new industrial
10        facilities.

11   Using the available sources of information, we develop a probability weighting for
12   expected sales to the customer. This probability weighting represents a risk
13   assessment of the likelihood of sales to existing customers continuing or sales to
14   potential future customers and expansions materializing. We consider timing risk
15   associated with the expected operational date for proposed new customers and
16   expansions. Where applicable, we also consider what portion of the customer’s
17   operations is likely to be electrified. The probability weighting is multiplied by the full
18   load anticipated to connect, resulting in a risk adjusted forecast.

19   Table A-1 shows the guideline framework for assigning probabilities to proposed
20   new large industrial loads for the reference load forecast scenario. Some criteria
21   outlined in the Probability Weighting Guide may not apply to all projects assessed.
22   For example, some projects may not declare a public final investment decision or
23   need to go through regulatory processes such as environmental assessments.
24   Professional judgement from our subject matter experts determines the final
25   probability weighting for projects.




                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                          Page 4

                                                                Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity

         Risk        Probability                               Description
      Assessment     Weighting
      Possible/     0-25%          The project is typically at early stages of development with respect
      Uncertain                    to engineering design, regulatory approval processes, economic

      Probable      50-75%         The project has typically achieved significant development

                                   in-service date.

4    A similar assessment is done for high and low load scenarios and load sensitivities
5    with more or less stringent criteria being applied. For example, a project assigned
6    25% in the reference load scenario might be assigned 0% in the low load scenario
7    and 50% in the high load scenario.

8    1.1.5        Light-Duty Electric Vehicles
9    The light-duty electric vehicle forecast is developed using a stock turnover model for
10   battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles weighing 4,500 kg or less. The model is
11   calibrated to actual vehicles registered in our service territory based on data from
12   Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (ICBC). From there the model forecasts
13   annual vehicle purchases and the electric vehicle market share to determine the


                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                  Page 5
                                                                                  Appendix A
                                                           Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    annual number of electric vehicles purchased. Market share may be developed
2    based on legislated zero-emission vehicles sales targets. For example, the High
3    Load Scenario assumes the B.C. Zero-Emission Vehicles Act (ZEV Act) targets are
4    met. The model uses this information to determine the cumulative number of electric
5    vehicles on the road. We then use an estimated distance driven per vehicle and
6    energy efficiency to determine the total load for all electric vehicles.

7    The light-duty electric vehicle model considers the entire provincial load. Electric
8    vehicle load in the FortisBC Inc. service area and the City of New Westminster is
9    removed, leaving the estimated BC Hydro service area load, which is allocated to
10   the residential and commercial forecasts. At the start of the forecast period the
11   allocation is approximately half to residential and half to commercial. By the end of
12   the forecast horizon this changes to approximately one third to residential and
13   two thirds to commercial based on charging type outlooks prepared by
14   BloombergNEF.

15   1.1.6       Other Sales
16   These loads include irrigation and street light customers, sales to other utilities (City
17   of New Westminster and FortisBC Inc.), firm exports (Seattle City Light and Hyder,
18   Alaska), and electricity used at BC Hydro owned facilities, such as distribution
19   substations. These forecasts are primarily developed using historical trend analysis
20   and information provided by the customers.

21   1.2         Peak Demand Forecast Methodology
22   Peak demand, measured in megawatts (MW), is the maximum expected amount of
23   electricity consumed in a single hour in any given year under an average cold
24   temperature assumption referred to as the design temperature. The design
25   temperature is the rolling average of the coldest daily average temperature over the
26   most recent 30 years. The BC Hydro system typically reaches its annual peak in the
27   early evening of a cold winter night. While some distribution substations are


                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                         Page 6
                                                                                Appendix A
                                                         Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    experiencing summer peaks due to space cooling load, at the system level
2    BC Hydro is a winter peaking utility and is expected to remain that way throughout
3    the forecast horizon. This is because our demand is more sensitive to colder
4    temperatures than warmer temperatures primarily due to electric space heating load.
5    For peak demand we refer to the forecast as “coincident” which means at the time
6    when our system is reaching its highest demand.

7    Figure A-2 below shows the build-up of the peak demand forecast.

8                     Figure A-2     Peak Demand Forecast Methodology




9    As depicted in Figure A-2, the total integrated peak demand forecast is an
10   aggregation of peak demand forecasts for distribution, transmission, and other
11   utilities and firm exports. In addition to the major components above, load additions
12   are made to account for codes and standards overlap, fuel switching, and line
13   losses.




                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 7
                                                                                                Appendix A
                                                                         Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    1.2.1          Distribution Peak Demand Methodology
2    The largest component of the peak demand is the distribution peak which is the total
3    peak demand for all distribution substations. Distribution peak demand is sensitive to
4    temperature due to space heating and cooling load.

5    The distribution peak forecast is developed using regional regression models which
6    consider historical distribution substation load and temperature data as well as the
7    forecasts of commercial and light industrial energy sales and the forecasted number
8    of residential accounts. We also consider distribution spot loads which represent
9    requests for service from potential large new distribution voltage customers.

10   Peak demand for electric vehicles and zero carbon building codes are forecasted
11   separately and included in the final distribution peak forecast.

12   1.2.1.1        Zero Carbon Building Code Peak Demand Methodology
13   The residential zero carbon building code peak uses load shapes based on heat
14   pumps applied to the number of new accounts expected to be built to zero carbon
15   building codes. The commercial zero carbon building code peak is forecasted using
16   its respective energy forecast multiplied by an energy-to-peak conversion factor.

17   1.2.1.2        Light-Duty Electric Vehicle Peak Demand Methodology
18   BC Hydro conducted load analysis of electric vehicle charging by charging type and
19   used the results of this analysis in our electric vehicle load forecast scenarios. Figure
20   A-3 below shows the hourly load shape by electric vehicle charging type based on
21   the average of four winter months system coincident peak days using metered data
22   from fiscal 2024. 1

4    As shown in Figure A-3, in fiscal 2024 home fast charging had the highest peak
5    demand and most charging was happening overnight, after 9:00 PM (hour 21). The
6    hourly electricity consumption forecast by charging type for future years was
7    determined using total electric vehicle annual energy forecast described above, the
8    proportion of annual energy by charging type, and hourly load profile by charging
9    type. These were then converted to coincident peak demands and the total
10   coincident peak demand for light duty electric vehicles was calculated as the sum of
11   the coincident peak demands for all charging types.

12   1.2.2             Transmission Peak Demand Methodology
13   The second largest component of the peak demand is the coincident transmission
14   peak demand which is the total coincident peak demand of all large industrial
15   customers connected to our system at transmission voltage.

16   The transmission peak demand forecast is prepared on an account-by-account basis
17   for all large industrial customers in the same manner described for the energy
18   forecast in methodology. These forecasts are aggregated into regional peak
19   forecasts which are used to determine a total BC Hydro coincident transmission
20   peak demand forecast.

                                    BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                                           Page 9
                                                                                  Appendix A
                                                           Load Scenarios and Load Sensitivity




1    1.2.3          Other Utilities and Firm Exports Peak Demand Methodology
2    Forecast demand for other utilities and firm exports are added to the total peak
3    demand forecast.

4    1.3            Distributed Energy Resources
5    The BCUC Planning Guidelines ask utilities to include a discussion or quantification
6    of the potential impact upon future demand of distributed energy resources which
7    are not influenced by the utility’s demand side management activities and are
8    outside of the utility’s direct control.

9    With the exception of industrial self generation, BC Hydro load forecast scenarios do
10   not consider load impacts of distributed energy resources which are outside of the
11   utility’s direct control and are not influenced by the utility’s demand-side
12   management activities. Additional distributed energy generation resources are
13   treated as initiated resources, or resource options, as appropriate, as outlined in
14   section 2.7.2 of the Application.

1    3.3          Future Resources
2    The Load Resource Balances above identify that additional resources beyond what
3    are contemplated by the near-term actions of the 2025 IRP may be required to meet
4    need under certain scenarios during the latter years of the planning horizon. These
5    have been identified as Future Resources in the Load Resource Balances. The
6    exact nature of these resources, such as whether they are additional demand side
7    options that may be identified in future integrated resource plans, facilities that
8    BC Hydro may construct or extend, or energy and capacity resources that BC Hydro
9    may enter into electricity purchase agreements will ultimately be determined in future
10   IRPs and acquisition processes. The resource options information used in the
11   2025 IRP and the portfolio modelling carried out indicate the following:

12   •     Future energy resources are most likely to be a mix of wind and solar with the
13         portfolio modelling indicating a likely mix of 25% solar and 75% wind;

14   •     The wind resources selected in the modelling were all on-shore wind and were
15         seen to be fairly distributed across the province with resources in the Peace
16         Region and North Coast being somewhat more prevalent;

17   •     Solar resources across several geographical regions were selected in the
18         modelling with the majority in the Kelly Nicola region;

19   •     The modelling indicated that other energy resources such as municipal solid
20         waste and run-of-river hydro could also play a minor role in the future resources
21         category; and

22   •     Future capacity resources could include options such as pumped storage hydro
23         and geothermal resources. As described in section 3.3.2, the 2025 IRP includes
24         a near term action to prepare to increase the availability of capacity resource
25         options through a Capacity Request for Expressions of Interest.

First Nations consultation
In conjunction with customer and public consultation, from May 2024 to September 2024, we consulted with First Nations on
what’s important to them with respect to the IRP. We used a variety of channels to notify and consult with First Nations which
allowed us to capture as many perspectives as possible. These channels included virtual sessions dedicated to hearing directly
from First Nations, one-on-one meetings with First Nations that were interested in learning more and providing input, a First
Nations survey that was developed with First Nations’ guidance, to capture input on the purpose of the IRP and its key elements,
and a dedicated email address for First Nations to contact us with questions or suggestions.


The table below describes what channels we used and how we communicated to participants.

 Channels we used

                       IRP First Nations webpage                                     information about the consultation process for the IRP and share
                                                                                     key upcoming dates for consultation.



                                                                                     We created an IRP email address and communicated with the
                       IRP First Nations email address                               200+ First Nations in B.C. via this email address. First Nations
                                                                                     could email us with questions or comments.


                                                                                     We created a First Nations survey to gather feedback. The
                                                                                     survey included an overview setting our planning context and
                       Online IRP survey                                             the questions were aimed at gathering information on the

What we heard
This section reports on what we heard from First Nations during Phase 1 consultation.

During Phase 1 consultation we heard from First Nations on planning considerations, energy management, and power supply
options. For the virtual information sessions, we provided materials with information on the purpose of an integrated resource
plan, things we consider when planning, and the different opportunities to meet customers’ long-term energy and capacity
needs using a variety of resources. Broad themes that emerged from the information sessions, one-on-one meetings, and the
survey are highlighted in this report. All supporting consultation materials, including presentation slides, can be found on
our website.

Planning considerations
The key topics raised in the information sessions under ‘Planning considerations’ were:

○ First Nations ownership—There is a keen interest amongst First Nations in ownership/economic benefits of projects coming
     out of the IRP near term actions. Interests included:
     ○ Clean energy projects coming out of the the Call for Power. Participants were interested in hearing more about the current
        Call for Power and shared considerations for future calls (e.g., sufficient time for meaningful consultation, lower minimum
          project size, types of technologies).
     ○ Interest in smaller projects outside of Calls for Power particularly for smaller Nations with less capacity.

○ L
   and and water impacts—In all information sessions, one-on-one meetings and in the survey results, we heard a consistent
  theme of the need for BC Hydro to limit impacts to land and water resources that have already been heavily impacted by past
  projects. Specifically, First Nations stated that:

     ○ B
        C Hydro should upgrade existing lines to accommodate higher demand before building new transmission lines and new
       routes to minimize impacts to the land.
     ○ BC Hydro should focus on increasing generation capacity at existing facilities versus building more dams or buying power
          from multiple independent power producers, as independent power projects have more impacts to land and water.
     ○ BC Hydro should do a deeper assessment of potential impacts as it relates to both project development and resource
          availability, particularly water.
     ○ BC Hydro’s plan should conform with First Nations’ stewardship plans.

     ○ BC Hydro should incentivize customers to use less energy instead of producing more energy.

○ Climate change—Participants are concerned about climate change and were interested in how climate change would be
     considered and addressed in the IRP.

○ Consultation—Participants expressed the importance of early and meaningful consultation on the IRP and on actions coming
     out of the IRP. Two specific ideas that were raised were:
     ○ Involve Elders/Knowledge Keepers in IRP consultation to gather unique perspectives.

     ○ Make one of the overall planning objectives to limit impacts to First Nations’ rights.

The key topics raised in the information sessions under ‘Planning Objectives’ were:

○ E
   nergy conservation—There was strong support from First Nations for energy efficiency activities and energy conservation
  programs if participation is voluntary and doesn’t penalize those that are unable to shift their electricity use.

○ Affordability—Affordability is a keen concern among First Nations and conservation incentives could help reduce costs.

○ R
   esource options—Participants expressed interest in different types of technologies, most notably smaller hydro, and tidal for
  future Calls and the benefits and opportunities of utility-scale batteries (energy sovereignty/ownership) for First
  Nations communities.

○ Infrastructure Resilience and Reliability—Some participants raised the need to consider issues of reliability and resilience in
   remote and end-of-line communities in the planning objectives.

First Nations survey results
For the First Nations survey, we presented questions in four sections:

1.	Planning considerations—Which of our planning priorities are most important to them (e.g., affordability, reducing greenhouse
    gas emissions, limiting land and water impacts or supporting the economy).

2.	Energy management—Which Demand Side Management options they prefer (e.g., solar, batteries, and programs and rates).

3.	Power supply options—What electricity supply options are preferrable (e.g., customer-based generation, BC Hydro-led
    generation, Independent Power Producer-led generation).

4.	Additional considerations—What BC Hydro should consider when drafting the IRP as it relates to the interests of First Nations
    and BC Hydro’s focus on reconciliation.


The results from the First Nations survey are summarized below.


Planning considerations:
When asked to rank four planning priorities, the majority of First Nations survey participants select ‘limiting land and water
impacts’ as their top choice:

Example comments:



      Limiting land and water impacts

     “Without land and water, there is no life, so we need to protect it before finding other ways to mitigate and adapt.
      Additionally, these land and water decisions should be made in meaningful collaboration with Indigenous right holder
      defined governments. Customers need to pay the “real cost of damages” which often do not include environmental,
      cultural and social impacts. If we take care of the above, B.C.’s economy will grow at a much steadier pace for a
      long term.”

     “Further impacts to the land and our climate must be mitigated as much as possible. That being said, many First Nation
      members struggle with low income or don’t have access to stable, good paying jobs; increasing energy costs adds stress
      to these members and their families. Economic growth for the province is important on some level, but cannot be
      prioritized above sustainability and proper stewardship of the land.”

     “As a First Nation, limiting environmental impacts is of primary importance to our community.”

     “Although I still feel strongly about the growth of B.C.’s economy and the stability of livelihoods for our citizens, I must
      emphasize the need to limit or eliminate land and water impacts in reflection of environmental stewardship. The existing
      transmission line has had various impacts to watercourses, wildlife, and territory access, and the community seems
      unforgiving of these transgressions, despite the other priorities and benefits listed.”


      Keeping costs down for customers

     “Rising costs are what affect our membership the most on a day-to-day basis.”

     “Consumers are already overtaxed on accommodations, clothing, and food. Any means necessary to keep costs down in
      order to be able to afford the necessities of life helps.”


      Reducing provincial GHG emissions through clean electricity

     “Climate change is already affecting land and water. Impacts need to be reversed from the top down.”


      Supporting the growth of B.C.’s economy

     “We need long term planning to provide continued development in B.C. while being price aware.”

     “B.C.’s economy is reliant on natural resources and more clean/cheap electricity enables development into more diverse
      areas. If we can keep costs down then that enables customers to use those funds elsewhere. We already have some of
      the cleanest electricity on the planet so that is seen as a low priority.”




Preference for keeping rates low vs. Proactively meeting future demand:

The majority of First Nations survey participants feel that BC Hydro should prioritize being ready to meet future demand (even it if
means customers may need to pay more). The remainder feel that BC Hydro should keep rates as low as possible and wait to
build new electricity resources.

     “BC Hydro should consider the environmental impacts its infrastructure has on First Nation lands, harvesting areas and

      Reasons for supporting

     “We all need to play our part in energy conservation, we cannot rely on just government and industry.”

      interest, then I immediately become adamantly opposed.”




Views on rate design:

When it comes to three possible ways BC Hydro could design rates, First Nations survey participants show a near-equal
preference for each option.


Number of respondents selecting


                     7                                                8                                 6


    BC Hydro should offer fewer rate choices. Most customers may have limited opportunities to change how they use
    electricity. Only some customers who can change how they use electricity from selecting these rate choices can
    save money. The amount of bill savings offered should be carefully managed.

    BC Hydro should actively encourage customers to participate in rates that reduce system costs. BC Hydro should
    provide several different rate choices, with higher bill savings opportunities, so that more customers use electricity
    in ways that reduce system costs. However, customers should have to opt-in to these rates.

    BC Hydro should take every step possible to reduce system costs through rates. Unless they opt-out, BC Hydro
    should put all customers on rates that encourage them to use electricity in ways that reduce system costs, even if
    some customers would pay more under that rate.

F I R S T N AT I O N S C O N S U LTAT I O N P H AS E 2 S U M M A RY R E P O R T

Summer 2025




Background
This report summarizes the Phase 2 consultation process and feedback received from First Nations on the 2025 IRP.


The consultation process
As part of the 2025 IRP development, during the spring and summer of 2024, we gathered input (Phase 1 of consultation) from
First Nations on various planning topics, including planning priorities. During the spring and summer of 2025, we gathered
feedback (Phase 2 of consultation) from First Nations on the key elements of the 2025 IRP. Feedback from both phases of
consultation was used to inform the development of our 2025 IRP.


What we did
All First Nations, including Tribal Councils, in the province were invited to participate in Phase 2 of consultation on the 2025 IRP.
BC Hydro also kept the First Nations Energy and Mining Council (FNEMC) apprised of the IRP consultation process and timeline,
and shared consultation materials. The FNEMC were invited to attend consultation sessions, in addition to their participation on
the 2025 IRP’s Technical Advisory Committee (TAC).


Forums we used

                                         On May 21, 2025, we notified all First Nations and Tribal Councils in the province that we were
                                         commencing Phase 2 consultation on the 2025 IRP, and that they were invited to attend one of
        Notification
                                         two virtual province-wide sessions or request a one-on-one meeting with BC Hydro. First
       of consultation
                                         Nations and Tribal Councils were sent a reminder on June 11, 2025 to register for a virtual session
                                         or request a one-on-one meeting.


         Consultation                    BC Hydro scheduled two 2-hour virtual consultation sessions on June 18 and June 24, 2025. The
           sessions                      PowerPoint presentation BC Hydro used during the sessions was posted on the 2025 IRP website.


             Survey                      An online survey was sent out on July 14, 2025, and remained open until August 13, 2025.


          One-on-                        BC Hydro offered to meet with any First Nation or Tribal Council about the 2025 IRP during the
        one meetings                     consultation period.


                                         BC Hydro had a dedicated email address (integrated.resource.plan.first.nations@bchydro.com)
   Written submissions
                                         set up and welcomed written comments throughout the consultation period.


   First Nations Energy                  BC Hydro contracted with FNEMC during Phase 1 consultation to review our survey and
        and Mining                       consultation materials and to brief the First Nations Leadership Council on 2025 IRP consultation-
     Council (FNEMC)                     related topics and invited FNEMC representatives to attend the virtual sessions in Phase 2.

                                                                                                                  Appendix C
What we heard
During the two First Nations virtual sessions, we described and sought feedback on the key elements of the 2025 IRP. First
Nations interests that emerged through these discussions were:


1. Interest in greater First Nations consultation, communication and inclusion

○ There was a need expressed for early, meaningful engagement respecting First Nations rights.

○ T
   here was strong support for meaningful collaboration with First Nations, including ownership, stewardship, and
  economic participation.

○ There was an interest for ongoing, transparent dialogue despite differing views.


2. Interest in understanding that BC Hydro is adapting to demand and technology

○ There was support for frequent updates to the IRP which are required to address technology changes and customer needs.

○ There was an interest in understanding how key industrial accounts influence demand forecasts.


3. Interest in environmental considerations

○ There was support for renewable energy only if environmental risks are mitigated, including impacts on water, wildlife, and
     cultural sites through all stages of renewable energy projects, including decommissioning.
○ Concern was expressed for First Nations communities which are directly impacted by environmental changes caused by hydro
     infrastructure, transmission lines, and ongoing development.
○ There was support for low-impact solutions, particularly upgrades over new builds.

   here was an interest in ensuring better coordination with government agencies on infrastructure and transmission works to
○ T
  reduce impacts.


4. Interest in energy sources, reliability & storage

○ There was support for backup power, battery storage, and geothermal—with caution about environmental risks.

○ There was support for diversified energy sources beyond wind and solar (geothermal, small nuclear, battery storage), with
     mixed views on wind and solar.
○ Interest was expressed in local storage solutions (e.g., home solar and batteries).


5. Interest in economic & social equity

○ There was interest in calls for smaller scale, locally led projects and tailored support for Nations with limited resources.

○ There was a desire to keep costs low.

○ There was support for local job creation and community-based energy generation.

Feedback from participants in one-on-one meetings included:

○ Support for acquiring additional renewable energy—and especially being able to participate in and receive economic benefits
     from the clean energy sector.
○ Support for customer solar.

○ Reflecting the changing climate in the 2025 IRP, such as prolonged droughts impacting reservoirs.

Feedback from FNEMC, received through participation in the TAC, are also considered here:

○ The requirements of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act must inform BC Hydro’s recommended actions
     in the 2025 IRP.

    BACKGROUND & OBJECTIVES

    BC Hydro’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) outlines how the utility will meet the
    province’s electricity needs over the next 20 to 30 years. In 2024, BC Hydro gathered input
    from stakeholder groups and First Nations across British Columbia and is now seeking
    feedback on key elements of the Plan.

    As part of this process, a survey was made available to the following groups:
        • BC Hydro Customers
       •   British Columbians (via a consumer panel and a public survey)
       •   First Nations
       •   Local Government

    The survey covers five elements:
       •   Customer solar program
       •   Acquiring additional renewable energy
       •   Upgrades to BC Hydro generating facilities
       •   Transmission reinforcements and expansions
       •   Preparing for new firm power sources

    This report includes feedback from First Nations. Feedback from Stakeholders are provided
    under a separate cover.

Background
We’re developing BC Hydro’s next Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), which is our 20-year strategy for the integrated power system.
The plan lays out actions to meet potential future growth in customer electricity needs through conservation and energy
management initiatives, upgrading BC Hydro’s generation and transmission assets, and power acquisitions. During the months
before BC Hydro is scheduled to file the IRP, we’re undertaking activities central to the development of the plan. This work is
divided into sections so that input from consultation and engagement can be incorporated into the planning to create a
comprehensive integrated resource plan.

○ E
   stablishing scope & gathering input: updating the data inputs that drive any changes to the existing plan; consulting with
  First Nations and engaging with our customers, the public and the Technical Advisory Committee.

○ A
   nalysis and trade-offs to develop the plan: modelling to produce plans that address a range of outcomes; working through
  a decision framework to consider future uncertainties and make trade-offs to develop base and contingency resource plans,
  and draft near-term actions.

○ R
   eview & incorporation of feedback into the final plan: a second round of engagement and consultation and additional
  analysis to refine the IRP; drafting of documents and submitting the next Integrated Resource Plan to the BC
  Utilities Commission.
○ Regulatory proceeding regarding the Integrated Resource Plan: once filed, a regulatory process to review the next
     Integrated Resource Plan will follow.

Consultation with First Nations and engagement with stakeholders (the public/customers and a technical advisory group) is a key
part of the process of developing an integrated resource plan. Our goal for the consultation and engagement activities is that
they be:

○ Accessible, such that it is simple and easy for British Columbians to participate,

○ Impactful, meaning input provided can be used to make informed decisions, and

○ Consistent across the engagement streams.

Phase One of engagement is now complete. Included in this report are key themes we heard from virtual sessions and the
Customer and Public surveys. A separate First Nations consultation summary report can be found here. The second phase of
engagement and consultation will occur in 2025 and will gather feedback on high-level key elements of the plan.




Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) | Gathering public and customer input for our IRP                                                 1

                                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application                        Page 3 of 84
                                                                                                                                                              Appendix D
What we did
From May 2024 until September 2024, we consulted with First Nations and engaged with various stakeholders, including
customers, gathering input for our IRP to understand how the priorities and values of British Columbians relate to BC Hydro’s
various planning topics. The public engagement stream includes BC Hydro customers1, members of the general public, and key
stakeholders such as local governments’ elected officials and staff, and interested associations. The table below describes the

forums provide qualitative perspectives and input. Broad themes running through the survey comments and forums are
highlighted in this report. All supporting engagement materials, including presentation slides and outstanding questions and
answers, are found at Public and customer engagement (bchydro.com).

                                                                                                                                          Appendix D
For the Customer and Public surveys, we presented questions in three sections:

1.	Planning considerations—Which of our planning priorities are most important to them (e.g., affordability, reducing greenhouse
    gas emissions, limiting land and water impacts, or supporting the economy).

2.	Energy management—Which Demand Side Management options they prefer (e.g., solar, batteries, and/or programs
    and rates).

3.	Power supply options—What electricity supply options are preferrable (e.g., customer-based generation, BC Hydro-led
    generation, Independent Power Producer-led generation).

For the virtual engagement sessions, we provided materials with information on the purpose of an integrated resource plan,
things we consider when planning, and the different opportunities to meet customers’ long-term energy and capacity needs
using a variety of resources. The information shared below summarizes both the survey and engagement session input.



Planning considerations

How BC Hydro customers consider planning priorities
When asked to rank four planning priorities, the majority of BC Hydro customers (54%) select ‘keeping costs down’ as their top
choice. The next biggest priority is for BC Hydro to reduce provincial greenhouse gas emissions through clean electricity (23%
ranking it number one). This is followed by limiting land and water impacts. Supporting the growth of BC’s economy is ranked as
the lowest priority.

      Keeping costs down for customers                                   54%                                    20%    17%         9%


     Reducing provincial greenhouse gas
                                                       23%                          23%                    25%          29%
      emissions through clean electricity




         Limiting land and water impacts         13%                    27%                                37%               29%


Supporting the growth of B.C.’s economy        10%                    30%                            21%              39%


                                                Ranked 1            Ranked 2              Ranked 3         Ranked 4

Numbers may not add up to exactly 100% due to rounding.




How the public survey respondents consider planning priorities
As reflected in their verbatim comments, public survey respondents tend to be particularly engaged on energy issues. Consistent
with this, of the four planning priorities, public survey respondents place the highest importance on reducing GHG emissions
through clean electricity (37% ranking it number one). This is followed closely by keeping customers’ costs down (ranked number
one by 32%). Limiting land and water impacts, and then supporting BC’s economy are their lowest priorities.

What’s most important to customers
Keeping costs down is the top priority across all customer groups. It’s particularly important to customers aged 45-64. For
customers, there are a few notable differences by region. BC Hydro customers on Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands are more
likely than customers in other areas of the province to prioritize environmental issues (reducing greenhouse gas emissions and
limiting land and water impacts). Meanwhile, customers living in the Lower Mainland are the most likely to prioritize supporting
B.C.’s economy. Other priorities for customers include:

○ Those who want BC Hydro to prioritize keeping costs down for customers feel that electricity is too expensive and that it
     would help with the rising cost of living. Customers older than 65 are especially likely to comment that keeping costs down is
     needed to help customers with limited incomes or on pensions (22%).
○ Customers who want BC Hydro to prioritize reducing provincial greenhouse gas emissions are concerned about climate
     change and global warming.
○ BC Hydro customers whose top priority is limiting land and water impacts feel it’s important to protect the environment and
     land and water from destruction.
○ Customers who want BC Hydro to prioritize supporting the growth of B.C.’s economy feel that it’s the most important thing
     to do.
○ Customers offer a variety of suggestions on what BC Hydro should consider when planning around potential climate impacts,
     the most common being that BC Hydro should add clean power generation such as wind and solar.
