What’s most important to respondents from the public
Reducing provincial greenhouse gas emissions is the top priority for public survey participants living on Vancouver Island and the
Gulf Islands, while keeping costs down for customers is the top priority for those living in the Interior and North. These two
priorities are ranked equally among public survey participants from the Lower Mainland. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is
particularly important to participants aged 18 to 44, while keeping costs down is ranked number one by those nearing retirement
age (55 to 64).

Participants with higher household incomes place the highest priority on reducing provincial greenhouse gas emissions, while
participants with lower household incomes place the highest priority on keeping costs down. Limiting land and water impacts is
also relatively important to this lower income group. Other priorities include:

○ P
   ublic survey participants who want BC Hydro to prioritize keeping costs down for customers say it’s important generally and
  feel that electricity is too expensive and that keeping costs down would help with the rising cost of living.

○ P
   ublic survey participants who want BC Hydro to prioritize reducing provincial greenhouse gas emissions are concerned about
  climate change and global warming.

○ P
   ublic survey participants whose top priority is limiting land and water impacts feel it’s important to protect the environment
  and minimize the negative impacts on natural resources.

○ P
   ublic survey participants who want BC Hydro to prioritize supporting the growth of BC’s economy feel that it’s the most
  important thing to do.

○ P
   ublic survey participants offer a variety of suggestions on what BC Hydro should consider when planning around potential
  climate impacts, the most common being that BC Hydro should add clean power generation such as wind and solar.

Customer comments about planning considerations



     “The cost and the environmental impacts need to be balanced. Costs are too high in areas like mine that do not have an
      alternative to electricity for heating.”

     “They are all important, BUT keeping costs down for customers is for me, the most important because people shouldn’t
      have to choose between groceries and temperature control in their homes in the temps we’ve been experiencing. I’m not
      concerned about comfort - I’m talking about the too cold and the too hot. We need also to consider the impacts on land
      and water - finding a way to live without leaving such a mark.”

     “Reducing greenhouse gas will ultimately serve all the other objectives, but has to be done without bankrupting
      current customers.”

     “The cost of our electricity is quite reasonable, so my priorities tend to be towards the environment.”

     “Reduced reservoir levels for hydro electricity and the need to diversify energy storage capacity to ensure adequate
      power availability even in drought years.”




Public respondent comments about planning considerations:



     “By keeping costs down for customers they will opt to use hydro over fossil fuels (industry, home heating, EV’s, etc.) so
      the two are hand in hand. One benefit should result in the other.”

     “If you can’t afford the electricity it doesn’t matter how carbon neutral it is.“

     “We are in a climate emergency. Decreasing climate impact should be everyone’s highest priority.”

     “Limiting land and water impacts while supporting GHG reductions should be the minimum requirements for our
      electricity system. It will save taxpayers/ratepayers in the long run by mitigating the negative effects on our natural
      resources and infrastructure.”

     “We need to spend money to maintain a reliable (hydro) electric system growing to meet future needs. Keeping costs
      down for customers is too short-range.“

     “We need to anticipate longer drought spells and threats to our water supply (diminished snowpack and less water
      captured in our reservoirs). Overall winter heating will likely decline, but cold spells can still put peak demand on our
      resources, so planning for sufficient resiliency in capacity remains important. Summer A/C use is likely going to increase.”

     “Local mini grids supported by solar, wind, water, etc. Energy generation and storage at all homes and businesses.”




Local government comments about planning considerations



     “The adequacy of distribution infrastructure should be included in the IRP.”

     “Large province-wide system has obvious efficiencies with regard to operations, technologies, etc, but could a reverse
      trend to form smaller entities to improve system security, small hydro plant operators with community management
      take place?”

     “I think it is important that the plan included diverse/distributed production and redundancy (especially for more remote/
      rural communities)”

                                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application                          Page 13 of 84
                                                                                                                   Appendix D
Considerations for planning around climate impacts
While we asked about our planning priorities, we also asked specifically about what customers and the public thought we should
be considering around the climate and the impacts of climate change. Customers offer a variety of suggestions, with the most
common being that BC Hydro should add clean power generation such as wind and solar.

The public respondents felt even more strongly about adding clean power generation with 37% choosing it as the top thing
BC Hydro should consider, and stating, as an example:

“Diversifying the energy sources (and locations) to ensure that our energy system is resilient and capable of adapting to
future impacts.”

  Comments—What BC Hydro should consider when planning around potential climate impacts
 Base: Customers who provided a comment                                                                                     533
 Adding clean power generation (e.g., wind, solar, etc.)                                                                    20%
 Adding more electricity generation capacity / demand is rising                                                             14%

Preference for keeping rates low vs. proactively meeting future demand
Amongst customer respondents, opinions are evenly split in terms of whether BC Hydro should keep electricity rates as low as
possible and wait to build new electricity resources or be ready to meet future electricity demand even if customers may need to
pay more.

The customer groups that are most focused on keeping rates low are those:

○ Living in the North and the Interior

○ Aged 45-64

○ With low household incomes.

The customer groups that are most focused on BC Hydro’s ability to meet future electricity demand are those:

○ Aged 65+

○ With high household incomes.

Energy conservation/management
The large majority of BC Hydro customers (86%) support energy efficiency activities and energy conservation programs. Even in
the North, where support trails behind other regions, 76% still support these types of activities and programs. Support for energy
efficiency activities and conservation programs increases with household income. The large majority of public survey participants
(88%) also support energy efficiency activities and energy conservation programs. Support is strong across all age groups, income

When it comes to customer and public views on three possible ways BC Hydro could design rates, they show a clear preference
(50%) for BC Hydro offering rate options that can lead to lower bills and reduced system costs—with these options being offered
on an opt-in basis.

The balance of both customers and the public are relatively evenly split between wanting BC Hydro to put all customers on rates
that will reduce system costs even if some customers would pay more and wanting BC Hydro to offer fewer rate choices because
not all customers are able to change how they use electricity.

Customers and the public in the North are most likely to feel BC Hydro should offer fewer rate choices, while younger customers
between 18 and 34 years old are the least likely to hold this viewpoint.

Deploying energy efficiency programs and energy generation resources
When it comes to building energy generation resources and scaling up energy efficiency programs, customers clearly show a
preference for BC Hydro balancing the development of energy generation resources and scaling up energy efficiency programs.
The option of scaling up energy efficiency programs and developing energy generation resources only when energy-efficiency
programs are no longer cost-effective is the least preferred option. Older customers (65+) and those living in the North are the

Battery storage technologies
Customers who ranked battery storage technologies as the most important feel that batteries have less environmental impact
and that it’s the best long-term solution because the technology will continue to develop. Public respondents said it’s flexible and
quick to deploy, it’s the best long-term solution because the technology will continue to develop, it can support local
infrastructure and has less environmental impact.


Customers



     “Battery storage may be easier to locate, easier to serve smaller regions, and available sooner than anything involving
      major construction. Less likelihood of falling behind the demand curve if construction takes longer than expected.”

     “We have to look toward the future, and battery storage of solar and wind should be great going forward.”

     “Smaller environmental footprint. Hopefully new technology will take care of battery manufacturing and storage.”




Public



     “Battery storage can occur anywhere, so more remote areas can retain any energy they produce (e.g., solar) and utilize it
      more effectively. There isn’t a need for 100s of km of transmission lines when the energy is being produced and
      stored locally.”

     “There is huge R&D now in the battery industry, including sodium- rather than lithium-based technologies. If large
      corporations like BC Hydro indicate their interest, it will further incentivize environmentally friendly battery tech.”

     “Battery storage is the most flexible since they can be moved around where needed, thereby reducing the need to install
      large transmission lines.

     “Anything to do with batteries is bad for the environment due to the mining and manufacturing of the batteries and the
      disposal after their limited lifetime “

     “Battery storage technology is still in its infancy. That may be a higher priority as the technology advances.”

                                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application                           Page 22 of 84
                                                                                                                      Appendix D
Pumped hydro storage facilities
Customers who ranked pumped hydro storage facilities as the most important chose this resource because it has the least
environmental impact and the most effective and reliable power production. They also feel that batteries have a negative
environmental impact. Public survey participants who ranked pumped hydro storage facilities as the most important chose this
because they consider it to be the most effective and reliable power production. They also feel that batteries have a negative
environmental impact.


Customer



     “I am skeptical of the long term (multi decade) suitability and environmental impacts of battery storage. Pumped storage
      is proven and reliable. It is also likely quicker to deploy in BC compared to new large scale transmission lines as its
      impacts are highly localized.”

     “Pumped hydro is the way to go. Closed loop, smaller impact than transmission lines, and batteries aren’t a good idea.
      Minerals, mining, disposals, efficiency.”




Public



     “Pumped water facilities more than likely have a longer life than batteries that wear out after so many charging cycles.”

     “Pumped hydro storage is well-established technology and will last for the life of the physical facilities. Large scale
      battery storage is still new technology with some uncertainty for cost and life of materials. New transmission lines
      occupy a lot of land and ‘waste’ energy.“

                                                                                                                       Appendix D
New transmission lines
Both the small group of BC Hydro customers and the small group of public survey respondents who ranked new transmission
lines as the most important resource did so primarily because they feel they create reliable infrastructure and cover the province.


Customer



     “New transmission lines are probably the most cost effective as a tried and true method. No faith in the large-scale
      manufacturing and disposal of the proposed batteries. Pumped hydro would likely have huge cost overruns as a new
      technology for BC Hydro.”

     “Transmission lines are already in place. It would seem to be the simplest and least expensive solution to augment the
      infrastructure already in place.”

     “Transmission lines have been around a long time and their impact and cost is understood. Newer technologies could
      have unforeseen and unintended consequences on the environment, cost-wise, etc.”




Public



     “Transmission lines are essential to keeping the grid intact and making everything work well. Pumped hydro storage
      seems necessary and useful, and battery storage seems like it could be bad for the environment.”

     “From your information Transmission lines appear to have the least damaging environmental effects.”

     “I don’t trust battery storage at this point, the mining of the items that are required to build the batteries and how to
      dispose of them when they are no longer useful.”

Summer 2025




The consultation process
As part of the 2025 IRP development, during the spring and summer of 2024 (Phase 1 of consultation), we gathered input from
the public on various planning topics, including planning priorities. During the summer of 2025, we gathered feedback (Phase two
of consultation) from the public on elements of the 2025 IRP.


What we did
In Phase 2 of consultation, which ran in July 2025, we gathered public feedback on elements of our 2025 IRP as well as the overall
plan. The public consultation stream included BC Hydro customers and consumer panel members, members of the general public
(through an IRP e-mail list), and local governments’ elected officials and staff. The table below describes the channels we used
and how we communicated to participants in Phase 2.

What we heard
During our consultation through the survey, we heard from the public on elements of the 2025 IRP as well as the overall plan. The
survey results provide a quantitative gauge on alignment in these areas, as well as qualitative input. The results of feedback
gathered through email written comments also provided qualitative perspectives and input.

Broad themes from the survey results are provided in the attached report.

Feedback was received from two local government organizations through email. In these submissions, concern was raised
regarding full environmental and economic costing of 2025 IRP elements. Interest was also expressed in having more information
about the 2025 IRP, improving coordination with local governments and affirming the role of electrification as a central strategy
for emissions reduction.

                                                                                                  Appendix D

    BACKGROUND & OBJECTIVES

    BC Hydro’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) outlines how the utility will meet the
    province’s electricity needs over the next 20 to 30 years. In 2024, BC Hydro gathered input
    from stakeholder groups and First Nations across British Columbia and is now seeking
    feedback on key elements of the Plan.

    As part of this process, a survey was made available to the following groups:
        • BC Hydro Customers
       •   British Columbians (via a consumer panel and a public survey)
       •   First Nations
       •   Local Government

    The survey covers five elements:
       •   Customer solar program
       •   Acquiring additional renewable energy
       •   Upgrades to BC Hydro generating facilities
       •   Transmission reinforcements and expansions
       •   Preparing for new firm power sources

    This report includes feedback from BC Hydro Stakeholders. Feedback from First Nations are
    provided under a separate cover.

COMPARATIVE OVERVIEW                                                                                                                                                   Appendix D

There is broad support for the 2025 IRP.
Among British Columbians (customers and panelists), support for the individual elements of the IRP ranges from 70% to 79%, with upgrades to generating facilities receiving the highest
level of support. Local governments are the most positive stakeholder group, with 83% in favour of the Plan overall and 78% to 88% supporting individual elements.

Over three-quarters of those who completed the Public Survey (77%), support the Plan. However, their support for Element 4 (Transmission Reinforcements & Expansions) is much lower
than their support for the other elements of the Plan.

                                                                                                                    Appendix D

          BRISH COLUMBIANS: SUBGROUP ANALYSIS

          Region
          Vancouver Island/Gulf Islands show the strongest support across all
          elements (residents of the Interior are equally supportive of Element 3).
          Lower Mainland and Interior are generally supportive but slightly less so
          compared to their Island counterparts. Northern B.C. consistently shows
          the lowest support and highest neutrality, especially for Element 5.

          Income*
          Higher-income (Not Qualified) respondents are more supportive than
          their Income Qualified counterparts. Lower-income (Qualified)
          respondents are more neutral and less supportive.

          2024 Call to Power Groups
          Group 2 (Non-Communities VI, SI, N) shows the highest support overall.

          Group 1 (respondents who reside in or near projects from the 2024 Call
          for Power (Communities)) is less supportive and more neutral.

          Group 3 (Non-Communities LM) falls in between, with moderate
          support across elements.



*Qualified (lower income) is defined as follows:
    • Household size=1 and household incomes is <$40,000
    • Household size=2 and household incomes is <$60,000
    • Household size=3 and household incomes is <$60,000
    • Household size=4 and household incomes is <$80,000
    • Household size=5 and household incomes is <$100,000   BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application    Page 82 of 84
    • Household size=6 and household incomes is <$100,000

                                                    Technical Advisory Committee Engagement




1    1            BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Technical
2                 Advisory Committee
3    The 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) was
4    established in March 2024 to provide technical advice and feedback from a group of
5    knowledgeable parties with experience relevant to BC Hydro’s resource planning to
6    support BC Hydro in developing a well-considered plan.

7    A draft Terms of Reference was circulated before the first meeting and finalized
8    following a comment period. Attachment A provides the final 2025 IRP TAC Terms
9    of Reference.

10   1.1          About the TAC Members
11   TAC members were chosen based on the following considerations:

12   •     Represent an organization or perspective that has a significant, province-wide,
13         policy-focused interest and stake in the 2025 IRP;

14   •     Have an interest and stake in the 2025 IRP that is broad as compared to having
15         a focus on a specific topic within the 2025 IRP;

16   •     As individuals, and the organization(s) they represent, have an in-depth
17         understanding of BC Hydro’s resource and electricity planning process, usually
18         demonstrated by involvement in previous British Columbia Utilities Commission
19         (BCUC) regulatory processes; and

20   •     Combined, represent a diversity of perspectives to support the development of
21         the plan.

22   Representatives from the following organizations were part of the TAC:

23   •     Association of Major Power Consumers (AMPC);

24   •     BC First Nations Energy and Mining Council (FNEMC);


                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 1
                                                                                 Appendix E
                                                   Technical Advisory Committee Engagement




1    •     BC Public Interest Advocacy Centre (BCPIAC);

2    •     BC Sustainable Energy Association (BCSEA);

3    •     Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP);

4    •     City of Vancouver;

5    •     Clean Energy Association of BC (CEBC);

6    •     Commercial Energy Consumers Association of BC (CEC);

7    •     Community Energy Association (CEA);

8    •     FortisBC (Gas & Electric);

9    •     Movement of United Professionals (MOVEUP);

10   •     Pembina Institute;

11   •     Residential Consumer Intervenor Association (RCIA); and

12   •     Urban Development Institute (UDI).

13   BC Hydro representatives chaired and moderated the TAC sessions. Staff
14   representatives from the Ministry of Energy and Climate Solutions, Climate Action
15   Secretariat, and the BCUC were invited to attend the TAC meetings as observers.

16   1.2         The TAC met between May 2024 and June 2025
17   The TAC met five times during the development of the 2025 IRP. All meetings were
18   conducted in a hybrid format, allowing both in person and virtual attendance.

19   •     May 8, 2024 (Meeting #1): topics included the policy and planning context for
20         the 2025 IRP, TAC workplan and schedule, prioritizing discussion topics for the
21         TAC, and engagement on load forecast scenario inputs;

22   •     June 14, 2024 (Meeting #2): topics included planning criteria and resource
23         adequacy, and resource options, both supply and demand;


                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                     Page 2
                                                                                            Appendix E
                                                              Technical Advisory Committee Engagement




1    •     September 9, 2024 (Meeting #3): this meeting was organized for the British
2          Columbia (B.C.) First Nations Energy and Mining Council to share an overview
3          of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
4          (UNDRIP) and to discuss reconciliation in the context of the energy industry;

5    •     November 1, 2024 (Meeting #4): topics included reconciliation with
6          presentations from TAC members that volunteered to share their organization’s
7          path to reconciliation, update on resource options, and planning criteria and
8          resource adequacy; and

9    •     June 21 & 23, 2025 (Meeting #5a & 5b): topics included review of the load
10         forecast scenarios/sensitivities, load resource balances (system and regional)
11         before planned resources, consideration of uncertainty in the 2025 IRP, and
12         review of 2025 IRP elements.

               2025 Integrated Resource Plan
               Technical Advisory Committee
                    Terms of Reference
A Technical Advisory Committee (herein referred to as the TAC) has been established to provide periodic
technical feedback on planning inputs, assumptions and analysis to BC Hydro during the development of the
2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP). Consultation with the TAC is part of a broader consultation process of the
IRP with First Nations, stakeholders, customers and the broader public.

Members of the TAC represent a subset and cross-section of knowledgeable participants. Specifically, TAC
members have been chosen considering the following reasons:

o They represent an organization or perspective that has a significant, province-wide, policy-focused interest
    and stake in the IRP.

o Their interest and stake in the IRP is broad – versus focusing on a specific topic within the IRP.
o Both they as individuals, and the organization(s) they represent, have an in-depth understanding of
    BC Hydro’s resource and electricity planning process, usually demonstrated by involvement in previous
    BC Utilities Commission regulatory processes.

o The TAC members represent a diversity of perspectives to support the development of a robust plan.
Government staff and BC Utilities Commission staff have been invited to attend TAC meetings as observers.

Decisions on membership will be made by BC Hydro.


Responsibilities of members
TAC members are requested to:

o Participate in all meetings. If the main TAC member is not able to attend, they will arrange to have their
    alternate attend on their behalf to ensure their organization is represented and to provide continuity
    throughout the process.

o Come prepared for discussions, which may include reviewing pre-meeting materials.
o Focus on issues associated with development of the IRP.
o Ensure that representations to the public are respectful of other TAC participants and other viewpoints raised
    in the process. Also, viewpoints should not be publicly attributed to individuals or organizations unless they
    have been expressed as “on the record.”


ALT E RNATES
Main members can designate alternates to represent them when they are unable to attend a meeting, or when an
alternate has more relevant knowledge or experience about a meeting topic. It is requested that if an alternate is
designated that they be briefed on previous discussions and materials prior to the meeting, and for the alternate
to report back to the main member on the meeting content and discussions. Alternates are welcome to attend
meetings with their main members; however, only the main members should participate in the discussions.


2025 IRP TAC Terms of Reference – September 2025                                                             Page 1 of 3

                     BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                         Attachment 1 - Appendix E




Responsibilities of BC Hydro
o Chair and moderate the meetings. This includes the following responsibilities:
   o   Develop overall workplan as well as individual meeting agendas.

   o   Prepare content of work brought to the TAC for review and discussion.

   o   Accountable for meeting notes and reporting.

   o   Run effective meetings in which mutual understanding is promoted and all members are given an
       opportunity to participate.

o Review and consider TAC members’ feedback in drafting the IRP, and where appropriate incorporate it.
o Report back on how TAC members’ feedback has been considered by BC Hydro.
o Post TAC meeting materials to the BC Hydro public website.


Process management

MEET INGS
Meetings will be either in-person (held in downtown Vancouver) or virtual. A draft agenda will be sent out in
advance of each meeting. Subject to change, BC Hydro anticipates about five to six meetings between May 2024
and March 2025.


MEET ING NOT ES
Meeting notes will provide a summary of TAC discussions, rather than transcribed notes with attribution. Meeting
notes will be distributed to TAC members in draft form after each meeting with a review and comment period for
accuracy, and will subsequently be published on the public BC Hydro IRP website.


T RANSPARENCY
Meeting agendas, presentations and supporting materials will be made publicly available shortly after the meeting
takes place. Meeting notes will be published on the public BC Hydro IRP website and will form part of the
consultation record.


COMMIT T EE MEMBER COMMENT S
At key junctures during the process, TAC members may be invited to provide attributed comments to BC Hydro
on core IRP topics to form part of the consultation record. Ministry and the BC Utilities Commission
representatives are exempt from this request.


EXPE NSES
BC Hydro will consider covering reasonable costs, e.g., travel expenses, for eligible TAC members located
outside of the lower mainland. Eligible TAC members may also be provided an honorarium for their time.

                                            Long-Run Marginal Costs and Market Price Forecast




1    1.1            An Introduction to Long Run Marginal Costs
2    BC Hydro’s energy and capacity Long Run Marginal Cost (LRMC) relate to the cost
3    of acquiring or developing new energy and capacity resources to meet incremental
4    demand. They include the costs of transporting that energy and capacity to the
5    Lower Mainland load centre, including costs associated with line losses and the cost
6    of incremental bulk transmission. The distribution and non-bulk transmission LRMC
7    relate to the cost of this type of infrastructure to serve incremental customer
8    demand.

9    The energy, capacity, and distribution & non-bulk transmission LRMCs, as well as
10   the market price forecasts, are inputs into BC Hydro’s reference prices. Reference
11   prices are a set of annual future cost benchmarks that are used for evaluating the
12   cost-effectiveness of BC Hydro’s business decisions including capital investments,
13   electricity purchase agreements, and demand-side measures (including rate
14   structures).

15   There are two types of long run marginal costs:

16   •     One set each for generation covering both energy and capacity; and

17   •     Another set for distribution and non-bulk transmission.

18   The 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) updates the LRMCs to:

19   •     $97/MWh for energy;

20   •     $300/kW-year for capacity; and

21   •     $110/kW-year for distribution and non-bulk transmission.




                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                       Page 1
                                                                                       PUBLIC
                                                                                   Appendix F
                                             Long-Run Marginal Costs and Market Price Forecast




1    1.2         Generation LRMC
2    The LRMC for energy and capacity is based on the cost of the incremental group (or
3    block) of generation resources that are available to meet future system energy or
4    capacity deficits.

5    1.2.1       Energy LRMC
6    The identification of the marginally priced generation resources to meet a future
7    need for energy has been informed by the results of the 2024 Call for Power. The
8    2024 Call for Power acquired new energy resources at a unit energy cost of
9    $77 / MWh, based on the average energy purchase agreement (EPA) cost of the
10   10 winning bids.

11   BC Hydro’s inventory of potential intermittent energy resource options described in
12   section 2.7.3 shows that onshore wind, followed by utility-scale solar, are the lowest
13   cost energy resources likely to be available. And as shown in Figure 2-12, there are
14   approximately 20,000 GWh of onshore wind energy resources available at a price
15   similar to the price observed in the 2024 Call for Power, which is a volume sufficient
16   to meet the energy need described in the 2025 IRP.

17   The energy LRMC is calculated based on the cost of energy delivered to the grid
18   plus the cost adjustments to account for additional costs of delivering the energy to
19   customers. Starting from the unit energy cost at the point-of-interconnection (UEC at
20   POI) and using the same categories of cost adjusters in the 2021 IRP, the updated
21   energy LRMC is $97/MWh in fiscal 2025 dollars, as shown in Figure F-1 below.




                          BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                        Page 2
                                                                                         PUBLIC

12   Request for Expression of Interest.


13   1.3        Non-Bulk Transmission and Distribution LRMC
14   This LRMC is the sum of the Non-Bulk Transmission Marginal Cost (NBTMC) and
15   the Distribution Marginal Cost (DMC) components, which are calculated using the
16   same general principleas the 2021 IRP with updated inputs and a revised
17   methodology for the DMC, as summarized further below.

18   1.3.1      Non-Bulk Transmission Component
19   The Discounted Total Investment Methodology (DTIM) used to calculate the NBTMC
20   factor remains unchanged from the Updated 2021 IRP.

21   The current NBTMC factor is based on non-bulk transmission line and substation
22   growth projects in BC Hydro’s Capital Plan between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2034. It
23   incorporates the January 2023 Reference Peak Forecast.

24   1.3.2      Distribution Component
25   In the Updated 2021 IRP, the distribution marginal cost factor was calculated using
26   the discounted cost of all incremental distribution assets and considering load


                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                       Page 5
                                                                                           PUBLIC
                                                                                       Appendix F
                                                 Long-Run Marginal Costs and Market Price Forecast




1    growth in a ten-year system load forecast as the denominator in deriving a cost per
2    kilowatt per year value. In the 2025 IRP, the methodology has been updated to
3    reflect the capacity contribution of the distribution assets as the denominator in
4    deriving a cost per kilowatt per year value. This change has been made as the
5    updated methodology has two advantages: (a) it is comparable to how unit capacity
6    costs are calculated for generation capacity and bulk transmission resource options;
7    and (b) it ensures that the values produced remain consistent and stable even when
8    load growth fluctuates throughout the years and varies unevenly across regions and
9    not always in lock step with the investments.

1    1.4            Market Electricity Price Forecast
2    Market electricity prices are used to value revenue from sale of surplus energy and
3    the cost of short-term imports under contingency scenarios and are an input into
4    BC Hydro’s reference prices.

5    British Columbia’s (B.C.’s) integrated electricity system is part of a larger
6    interconnected grid called the Western Interconnection, which includes Alberta and
7    14 western U.S. states. Utilities in the Western Interconnection trade energy in a
8    variety of markets. BC Hydro purchases energy from and sells energy to Powerex
9    Corp (Powerex) at the B.C. border pursuant to the Transfer Pricing Agreement
10   between BC Hydro and Powerex. The relevant market index for the Transfer Pricing
11   Agreement is the Mid-Columbia (“Mid-C”) trading hub.

12   Section 6.2 of the 2021 IRP provides a description of how a forecast of the Mid-C
13   market price is developed. For the 2025 IRP, the forecast methodology is largely
14   unchanged. 2 The underlying hourly market price forecast has been updated with the
15   Hitachi 2024 Spring Market Price Forecast and BC Hydro has made one
16   methodological change which is that we no longer apply a negative price adjustment
17   because the Hitachi 2024 Spring Market Price Forecast included negative pricing.

18   Figure F-3 below presents the annual average BC Hydro market price forecast at
19   Mid-C under reference, high-gas price, and low-gas price scenarios.

1    1              Introduction
2    This Appendix provides a high-level description of BC Hydro’s approach to
3    transmission (bulk and non-bulk), distribution, and substations planning.


4    2              Load Scenarios and the IRP are Key Inputs to Power
5                   System Planning
6    The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) and its load scenarios and sensitivities are key
7    inputs used for the planning of BC Hydro’s power system. Figure G-1 below shows
8    the dependence of transmission, distribution and substation planning on the load
9    scenarios and the IRP.

10                          Figure G-1          Power System Planning use of Load
11                                              Scenarios1 and Resource Plans




12   Following the development of an IRP, a series of system studies and assessments
13   are completed, including a Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) system
14   impact study and facilities study for the reference load scenario, to identify any major
15   bulk transmission system reinforcement requirements over the 20-year planning


     1   In addition, actual feeder loadings are used in distribution feeder planning.



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                   Page 1
                                                                                             Appendix G
                                                       Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    horizon, and any non-bulk transmission system reinforcements over the 10-year
2    planning horizon. Subject to BCUC approval, similar studies are completed for the
3    high load scenario and any load sensitivities (when applicable). These studies allow
4    for the development of transmission plans that identify bulk and non-bulk
5    transmission system reinforcements that may be needed to reliably provide the
6    necessary transmission service under various scenarios. Depending on the timing of
7    the need, capital investments may be recommended, which will also be included for
8    prioritization as part of BC Hydro’s annual capital planning process.

9    Typically, BC Hydro prepares load forecast scenarios for the integrated system
10   peak2 demand and distribution substation load forecasts on an annual basis, which
11   are used to assess bulk and non-bulk transmission, distribution and substation
12   system needs on an ongoing basis. As part of the integrated system peak demand
13   load forecast scenario development, area guidelines3 are created which are used in
14   the development of a distribution substation load forecast, that is weather
15   normalized,4 for individual substations. Upon receipt of the area guidelines, the
16   development of the substation load forecast is completed and includes all load
17   forecast scenarios. Transmission, distribution, and substation studies are completed
18   using these load forecasts (load forecast scenarios and the distribution substation
19   load forecast scenarios) to compare the expected system load growth against the
20   system capability, to determine the location and nature of any system constraints.
21   The nature of these system constraints varies case by case, but generally involves
22   thermal overload, voltage out of acceptable range, voltage instability, or angle



     2   System upgrades are driven by the annual peak demand. Once the system is designed to meet the peak
         demand, it is capable of delivering the electricity required to meet the annual energy demand.
     3   In alignment with the load scenarios, guidelines are developed for 15 areas to provide top-down direction for
         the development of the distribution substation load forecast scenarios.
     4   In order to account for year-to-year variation in temperatures and other impacting factors, the historical
         substation peak demand data is ‘normalized’ to remove the impact of temperature variation from the mean
         temperature and, where possible, the impact of day of week, holidays, hours of darkness and other factors
         that may impact the peak demand.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                              Page 2
                                                                                               Appendix G
                                                         Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    instability5 during various load or generation dispatch conditions and under specific
2    contingencies. Solutions to resolve constraints within the 10-year planning horizon
3    are then recommended, which form the basis for projects that are prioritized as part
4    of BC Hydro’s annual capital planning process.

5    BC Hydro’s Capital Plan provides a view of the projected bulk and non-bulk
6    transmission, distribution, and substation investments that have been prioritized for
7    action within the planning horizon. A summary outlining BC Hydro’s most recent
8    Capital Plan is included as part of BC Hydro’s Revenue Requirements Applications,
9    providing an opportunity to review investments driven by BC Hydro’s long-term
10   system planning. BC Hydro also files applications with the BCUC for capital projects
11   that exceed the major project thresholds. In addition, BC Hydro provides an annual
12   forecast of anticipated major capital project filings.


13   3              BC Hydro’s Approach to Power System Planning
14   BC Hydro assesses the needs of the power system on an ongoing basis and, where
15   needed, develops or modifies short to long term plans to meet current and future
16   load requirements. Figure G-2 below provides an overview of some of the typical
17   inputs used during transmission, distribution, and substation planning.




     5   Angle instability or rotor angle instability refers to the loss of synchronism between generators following a
         power system disturbance.



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                                 Page 3
                                                                                    Appendix G
                                              Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1                      Figure G-2      Typical System Planning Inputs




2    The sub-sections below provide additional details on BC Hydro’s approach to
3    transmission, distribution, and substation planning.

4    3.1          Transmission Planning
5    The transmission planning process considers multiple planning objectives and
6    strategies, such as:

7    •     Ensuring supply safety, reliability, and affordability;

8    •     Applying life-cycle asset management principles to get the most of our existing
9          system;

10   •     Providing operational flexibility and ensuring capacity adequacy;

11   •     Coordinating bulk system needs and regional system demands;

12   •     Supporting resource planning optimization for both the resource side and
13         demand side;


                          BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                        Page 4
                                                                                 Appendix G
                                           Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    •    Providing strong system reinforcement justifications that consider system risk
2         and load and resource uncertainties; and

3    •    Meeting the requirements of reliability standards and performance criteria.

4    Examples of transmission planning studies include long-term NITS studies,
5    long-term Firm Point-to-Point studies, annual mandatory reliability standards (MRS)
6    compliance assessment studies, capital planning studies, and interconnection
7    system impact studies, covering both bulk and non-bulk transmission system. If any
8    of these analyses indicate that the existing power system cannot meet the requested
9    transmission service, reinforcement alternatives are investigated through these
10   studies. The reinforcement alternatives considered at the bulk and non-bulk
11   transmission planning levels include optimizing the existing system wherever
12   possible, non-wires alternatives to system expansion (such as reactive power
13   support), and upgrades and expansion of the transmission system when required.

14   3.1.1      Bulk Transmission System Studies
15   BC Hydro’s bulk transmission system includes all 500 kV transmission system
16   assets, and some 230 kV transmission system assets in the Selkirk area as well as
17   the assets supplying electrical power to Vancouver Island. The primary function of
18   BC Hydro’s bulk transmission system is to transfer power and energy over long
19   distances from remote network resource clusters to network load centers.

20   Bulk transmission system studies are long-term planning studies focused on the bulk
21   system, usually covering a planning horizon of 20 years or more. The capacity of the
22   bulk transmission system is evaluated by considering the transfer capability at
23   certain defined locations called cut-planes. The integrated system coincident peak
24   demand load scenarios and the distribution substation load forecast are modeled for




                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                       Page 5
                                                                                             Appendix G
                                                       Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    bulk transmission planning studies, and network resources are dispatched based on
2    the latest generation dispatch in transmission planning guidelines.6

3    3.1.2          Non-Bulk Transmission System Studies
4    BC Hydro’s non-bulk (or regional) transmission system includes its 360 kV, 287 kV,
5    230 kV (excluding assets in the Selkirk area), 138 kV, 132 kV, and 66 kV
6    transmission system. It interconnects with BC Hydro’s Bulk transmission system and
7    regional network resources and delivers power to BC Hydro’s distribution system,
8    and to transmission voltage customers.

9    Non-bulk transmission system studies are medium to long-term planning studies and
10   can generally cover a planning horizon of 10 or more years. Non-bulk transmission
11   system studies are completed to support annual processes such as MRS
12   compliance assessments, capital planning studies, and interconnection system
13   impact studies. The distribution substation load forecasts that are developed based
14   on area guidelines aligned with the integrated system peak demand load scenarios,
15   transmission voltage customer peak load scenarios, and plan elements of the
16   integrated resource plan serve as the basis for determining the needs of the
17   non-bulk transmission system.

18   3.2            Distribution Planning
19   Relative to the other power system portfolios, the distribution system is the most
20   dispersed across the province, with the highest number of assets and the highest
21   number of interactions with customers and the public. The distribution system is
22   continually evolving as it is expanded and upgraded to connect new customers and
23   maintained to ensure safe and reliable service. The distribution planning process
24   considers multiple planning objectives and strategies, such as:




     6   Refer to Appendix H-3 of the Original Application in the 2021 IRP.



                             BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                 Page 6
                                                                                   Appendix G
                                             Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    •    Supplying customers with safe, reliable, and clean power;

2    •    Applying life-cycle asset management principles to get the most of our existing
3         system;

4    •    Supporting the interconnection of residential, commercial, and light industrial
5         loads, and distributed energy resources;

6    •    Meeting safety, reliability, power quality, environmental and other regulatory
7         standards; and

8    •    Integrating and coordinating with the upstream electrical supply from
9         substations and the associated transmission system.

10   3.2.1       Distribution System Studies
11   The distribution substation load forecast is used to identify areas with distribution
12   substation constraints, identify capital projects required to transfer load between
13   substations, evaluate available substation and feeder section capacities when
14   responding to new customer connection requests, and to identify the potential need
15   for new feeder positions.

16   To align with larger system plans, distribution projects will undergo integrated
17   planning with substations and transmission planning, when warranted. Distribution
18   projects requiring integrated planning may include duct bank egress from
19   substations, new feeder projects, and feeder voltage conversion projects to upgrade
20   distribution voltage levels to 25 kV.

21   To identify feeder capacity constraints, actual feeder loading is reviewed in
22   comparison to feeder capacity limits. To address feeder capacity constraints,
23   potential solutions may include one or a combination of the following:

24   •    Load Transfer: Reconfiguring feeders to transfer load from heavily loaded
25        feeders to adjacent feeders with available capacity;



                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                        Page 7
                                                                                   Appendix G
                                             Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    •     Equipment Upgrade: Upgrading undersized distribution equipment, such as
2          overhead conductors or underground cables;

3    •     Voltage Conversion: Performing feeder voltage conversion (e.g., from 12 kV
4          to 25 kV);

5    •     Demand Side Management and Distributed Energy Resources: Pursue
6          demand side measures and/or distributed energy resources that offer local
7          peak capacity to defer or eliminate the need for distribution upgrades; and

8    •     New Feeder: Constructing a new feeder from the substation.

9    This assessment is further validated through additional feasibility studies, field site
10   visits, and input from various groups across BC Hydro such as field operations,
11   engineering, indigenous relations, properties, and environment.

12   3.3          Substation Planning
13   Substation plans are developed to address transmission and distribution system
14   requirements. The substation planning process considers multiple planning
15   objectives and strategies, such as:

16   •     Supplying customers with safe, reliable, and clean power;

17   •     Applying life-cycle asset management principles to get the most of our existing
18         system;

19   •     Addressing the needs identified through various transmission and distribution
20         planning studies; and

21   •     Meeting safety and reliability standards, availability requirements, regional
22         adequacy guidelines, efficiency needs, environmental requirements, security
23         standards, and other requirements.




                         BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                         Page 8
                                                                                    Appendix G
                                              Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    3.3.1       Substations Studies
2    On an annual basis, the firm capacity of BC Hydro’s distribution substations is
3    reviewed so that the capacity ratings reflect the current station configuration and
4    equipment ratings. The distribution substation load forecast is compared to the firm
5    capacity of each substation to determine if the substation will have adequate
6    capacity over the forecast period to meet our customers’ needs. For new feeder
7    positions, the existing and ultimate station configuration and layout are reviewed to
8    determine the potential options to meet the need for new distribution feeders. Some
9    potential solutions to address the need for additional station capacity and/or feeder
10   positions include:

11   •    Load transfer: Transfer load amongst adjacent substations to mitigate
12        overloaded substations, although this is generally a short-term solution;

13   •    Add feeder positions: Add feeder positions in existing substations to mitigate
14        feeder overloading, improve reliability, and utilize existing station capacity;

15   •    Voltage conversion: Convert substation distribution voltage from 12 kV
16        to 25 kV, which increases feeder capacity and addresses reliability issues;

17   •    Upgrade substation: Upgrade existing substations by adding capacity and
18        feeder positions to address medium- and long-term distribution capacity needs;
19        and

20   •    Construct new substation: Build a new substation if the capacity of the
21        existing stations in the area are inadequate to meet medium- and long-term
22        needs. New substations are planned to meet long-term needs, typically over a
23        20-to-30-year period, for both transmission and distribution.

24   If the solution alternative includes transmission work, BC Hydro produces station
25   one-lines and high-level equipment specifications to meet all transmission planning
26   criteria and strategies. For new substation construction, the future requirements for



                          BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                        Page 9
                                                                                          Appendix G
                                                    Transmission and Distribution Planning Processes




1    substations, transmission and distribution are considered, allowing for the
2    development of ultimate stage plans for the substation including ultimate stage one-
3    line diagrams.

1    4.1           Distribution System Impacts under Various Load Forecast
2                  Scenarios
3    As described in section 2.5.2, the High Load Scenario assumes additional large
4    industrial development reflecting economic growth and diversification of trade and
5    faster adoption of light-duty electric vehicles in the near to medium term. A need for
6    more distribution infrastructure, compared to the need under the Reference Load
7    Scenario, could arise in areas where load growth is driven by these factors. In
8    particular, the need for distribution infrastructure is sensitive to the rate of adoption
9    of electric vehicles. The need and timing for any distribution infrastructure will be
10   determined through the distribution studies described above and will also depend on
11   the available capacity of distribution infrastructure in areas where load growth
12   occurs.

13   The High Load Scenario assumes a stronger outlook for large industrial customers
14   involved in natural gas processing, liquified natural gas exports, and mining. These
15   loads are not typically connected to the distribution system and therefore no impacts
16   on distribution infrastructure are expected if these loads materialize. This is also the
17   case the for the North Coast Load Sensitivity which reflects large industrial load
18   growth potential in the North Coast region.

                                                   Methods for Assessing Resource Uncertainty




1    1           Introduction
2    This Appendix focuses on the quantitative aspects of estimating uncertainty, building
3    on the techniques identified and explored in BC Hydro’s 2013 Integrated Resource
4    Plan (2013 IRP) and the 2021 Integrated Resource Plan (2021 IRP). Detailed
5    discussions of these techniques and supporting literature can be found in those
6    earlier documents. What has changed in this Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) is the
7    expanded scope of uncertainty quantification to include supply-side resources
8    (previous IRPs focused on quantifying uncertainty around demand-side resources
9    only). This Appendix catalogs the resources included in the uncertainty assessments
10   and provides a detailed exploration of the results.

11   As in previous IRPs, the ultimate metric is a proxy for risk, referred to as the Risk of
12   Resource Under-delivery. This metric estimates the potential divergence between
13   our planning and actual resource acquisitions, in terms of both energy (GWh/year)
14   and capacity (MW). More specifically, it is defined as the difference between the
15   “mid” outcome and the “downside” outcome within a probability distribution. As in
16   previous IRPs, the “mid” outcome is the average of the middle 60% of the
17   distribution and the “downside” outcome is the average of the lower 20% tail.

18   The metric considers the risk of costs impacts to customers from resource
19   under-delivery which could require mitigation efforts by BC Hydro, such as acquiring
20   higher-cost resources to fill the gap. To simplify the analysis, this metric is applied to
21   a single year, fiscal 2035, which is far enough in the future to provide insight into the
22   potential magnitude of uncertainty without being so far out that it becomes overly
23   speculative.


24   2           A Brief Recap of Methods for Assessing Uncertainty
25   This section provides a brief overview of the methods used to quantify uncertainty
26   and generate the Risk of Resource Under-delivery metric for the 2025 IRP:


                        BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                         Page 1
                                                                                Appendix H
                                                 Methods for Assessing Resource Uncertainty




1    •   Eliciting subjective probability estimates: When long-term planning
2        variables are difficult to quantify, professional judgement is used to develop
3        probability estimates. These may apply to binary outcomes or to ranges of
4        parameter values;

5    •   Accounting for portfolio effects when aggregating estimates: Where
6        warranted, professional judgement is also used to account for correlations
7        among uncertain variables; and

8    •   Creating probability distributions by combining estimates: The estimates
9        from the previous steps are used in Monte Carlo simulations to generate
10       probability distributions. These distributions illustrate both the cumulative impact
11       on the range and the likelihood of different outcomes for individual variables
12       and their aggregate.


13   3            Demand-Side Measures Assessed for this IRP
14   The following demand-side measures were included in the uncertainty assessment
15   of planned savings:

16   •   Energy Efficiency Programs;

17   •   Customer Solar Programs;

18   •   Industrial Load Curtailment Programs;

19   •   Demand Response Programs; and

20   •   Rates.


21   4            Supply-Side Measures Assessed for this IRP
22   The following resources and characteristics were included in the uncertainty
23   assessment:

24   •   EPA Renewals;


                       BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                      Page 2
                                                                                 Appendix H
                                                  Methods for Assessing Resource Uncertainty




1    •    Energy acquisitions; and

2    •    Effective Load Carrying Capability for Wind projects.

3    While the inclusion of supply-side resources in the formal uncertainty assessment is
4    new for this IRP, the technique of using subjective probability elicitation to capture
5    BC Hydro’s professional judgment is consistent with the approach described in
6    previous IRPs and the assessment of uncertainty for demand-side management
7    savings.

8    Planning for energy and capacity from projects acquired through the Call for Power
9    or other power acquisition processes introduces several uncertainties, including:

10   •    Attrition risk: Whether projects reach commercial operation;

11   •    Schedule risk: When projects reach commercial operation; and

12   •    Performance risk: How much electricity they ultimately produce.

13   For yet to be constructed projects under new electricity purchase agreements,
14   BC Hydro estimates an attrition rate of 30%. This estimate is based on BC Hydro’s
15   experience from prior calls and also takes into consideration certain publicly
16   available information of recent calls for power from other jurisdictions in Canada,
17   reflecting our current view of our procurement processes and market conditions.
18   Given the multiple factors that can impact a yet to be constructed project, this
19   attrition risk estimate is uncertain.

20   To assess the attrition risk for a group of potential projects, each project was treated
21   as a binary variable with a 70% probability of reaching commercial operation.

3    This same analysis also tracked the capacity contribution of new wind projects,
4    recognizing that their Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) is highly uncertain.
5    This uncertainty is largely driven by whether new wind projects are geographically
6    dispersed or concentrated in a single region. Geographically dispersed projects have
7    a higher ELCC while concentrated projects have a lower ELCC. This is because
8    dispersed projects are more likely to be generating when needed. If wind is not
9    blowing in one area, it could still be blowing in another.

10   As discussed in section 2.4.2.3 BC Hydro has assumed an ELCC for wind of 0.24 or
11   24%. A distribution of possible ELCC values was constructed, ranging from zero to
12   up to roughly 0.4. This was used as an input to Monte Carlo simulations along with
13   project attrition to generate a distribution of capacity contribution arising from new
14   energy projects selected through portfolio modelling.

4    7           Additional Uncertainties of Note – Avoided
5                Transmission and Distribution Benefits
6    One of the key benefits of implementing demand-side measures is the potential to
7    defer or eliminate the need for investments in transmission and distribution
8    infrastructure. For the 2025 IRP, BC Hydro updated its methodology for estimating
9    these avoided costs below the bulk transmission level. Details of this updated
10   calculation can be found in Appendix F, section 1.3.

11   Recognizing that these estimated savings are subject to uncertainty, BC Hydro
12   conducted sensitivity analysis to determine whether the comparison of DSM options
13   is affected by difference assumptions for avoided transmission and distribution
14   costs.

15   A range of potential avoided transmission and distribution benefit values was
16   assessed. From this range:

17   •    The “Low” value corresponds to the P10 (10th percentile);

18   •    The “High” value corresponds to the P90 (90th percentile), and

19   •    The “Best Estimate” represents the central value.

2. Gross Demand Forecasts

     a. Utilities should develop a minimum of two gross       Section 2, subsection 2.3
        demand forecasts or scenarios (i.e. forecasts         Appendix A, section 2.
        before any estimated reductions from
        demand-side measures) for both annual and
        peak demand, which illustrate a reasonable
        range of potential outcomes. The number of
        forecasts or scenarios should balance the need
        to adequately illustrate demand uncertainties,
        while avoiding excessive complexity. Forecasts
        should be presented with a breakdown by
        customer class. Utilities should briefly explain
        whether any of the forecasts or scenarios are
        considered more likely, either in quantitative or
        relative terms.

     b. LTRPs should include a description of the             Section 2, subsection 2.3.5
        methodological approach used for demand               Appendix A, section 1
        forecasting, and explanation of the key
        assumptions underpinning the forecasts. For           Peak demand: Appendix A, section 1.2.
        peak demand, this should include the
        assumptions used to estimate peak weather
        conditions.

     c. Electric utilities should also include a discussion   Appendix A, section 1.3.
        or quantification of the potential impact upon
        future demand of distributed energy resources
        which are not influenced by the utility’s
        demand-side management activities and are
        outside of the utility’s direct control.

     d. Utilities should include discussion or analysis to    Section 2, subsections 2.3.1 and 2.9.3.
        illustrate the most significant drivers of
        uncertainty associated with the demand
        forecasts and scenarios, and how these have
        been addressed in the LTRP.

   explanation of whether there is sufficient
   information available in the LTRP to enable the
   BCUC to make a determination under
   section 44.1(9); ii. Evidence that parties that
   may be directly affected by the BCUC’s
   determination under section 44.1(9) have been
   provided adequate notice or the opportunity to
   participate or be represented in the proceeding;
   and iii. A discussion of whether and how a
   BCUC determination under section 44.1(9)
   would promote regulatory efficiency by reducing
   the scope or eliminating the need for future
   BCUC proceedings, without unduly expanding
   the scope of the BCUC’s review of the LTRP.

d. The BCUC recognizes there is a risk that            Cover Letter.
   information filed in an LTRP may become
   out-of-date during lengthened regulatory
   proceedings. Accordingly, the BCUC aims to
   review LTRPs in an efficient and timely manner.
   In LTRP applications, utilities are encouraged to
   propose a regulatory review process that
   balances efficiency with the need for open and
   transparent hearings. Utilities are also

   encouraged to provide supporting information to
   justify any proposals for a limited regulatory

1    1              Demand-Side Measures Key Assumptions
2    This Appendix provides details on the demand-side measures resource options and
3    the key assumptions used in their development.

4    We have also included details on some of the initiated demand-side measures,
5    where the same methodology or model was used to update information for the
6    2025 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), or where the initiated resource was a key
7    component in the methodology for developing the resource option for the 2025 IRP.

8    1.1            Energy Efficiency
9    The energy efficiency resource option in the 2025 IRP (Energy Efficiency
10   Programs B) is substantially the same as the “Higher Plus” resource option included
11   in the Updated 2021 IRP.

12   For the 2021 IRP, the energy efficiency resource options1 were developed using
13   results from the Energy Efficiency Conservation Potential Review2 study. This study
14   characterized hundreds of energy conservation measures across all sectors and
15   estimated the theoretical potential that is technically possible. The resource options
16   were based on market potential, which is primarily driven by two key parameters:
17   customer economics and adoption rates of new products.3




     1   Energy Efficiency Resource Options in the 2021 IRP can be found in Appendix J to the 2021 IRP. Full details
         on approach and methodology for the Energy Efficiency Resource Options was provided in Appendix K to
         the 2021 IRP: https://docs.bcuc.com/documents/proceedings/2021/doc_65194_b-1-bch-
         integratedresourceplan-public.pdf.
     2   This study was originally completed in 2017 and updated in 2020 to inform the 2021 IRP.
     3   Product adoption was projected using a bass diffusion model of how new products get adopted into a
         population via an S-shaped adoption curve that is based on observed experience with new products in
         several sectors.

1    For the 2025 IRP, a small number of high-level adjustments were made to the
2    savings and costs of the initiated resource, Energy Efficiency Programs A,4 and the
3    resource option, Energy Efficiency Programs B, to reflect material changes since the
4    Updated 2021 IRP.

5    The adjustments to savings were:

6    •     Industrial sector: Savings were reduced to align with changes in the large
7          industrial load forecast. Specifically, savings in the pulp and paper and wood
8          sectors were reduced, while savings in the mining sector were increased.
9          However, because the pulp and paper and wood sectors previously accounted
10         for a larger share of savings, the net effect was a reduction in savings. As a
11         result, industrial sector savings are approximately 15% lower for both Energy
12         Efficiency Programs A and Energy Efficiency Programs B compared to the
13         Updated 2021 IRP; and

14   •     Commercial sector: Savings from lighting technologies were reduced to reflect
15         widespread market transformation in this area.5 Overall, commercial sector
16         savings are approximately 12% lower for Energy Efficiency Programs A and
17         15% lower for Energy Efficiency Programs B compared to the Updated
18         2021 IRP.

19   Additionally, the costs were increased by 15%6 to account for inflation since the
20   Updated 2021 IRP.




     4   Energy Efficiency Programs A is based on the “Higher Energy Efficiency” option selected in the Updated
         2021 IRP, and reflects incentive levels of approximately 80% of incremental customer cost for energy-saving
         measures.
     5   Many customers are adopting efficient lighting technologies without the need for support from DSM
         programs, and improved efficiency in commercial lighting is reflected in the before-DSM load forecast
         scenarios.
     6   In line with the BC Stats Consumer Price Index.

1    1.2         Demand Response
2    The demand response resource option in the 2025 IRP (Demand Response
3    Programs B) was developed by using the initiated resource (Demand Response
4    Programs A) as a basis, then adjusting costs and savings at a high-level to reflect
5    increased incentives and participation.

6    The initiated resource (Demand Response Programs A) was updated relative to the
7    resource option included in the 2021 IRP, through an updated Demand Response
8    Potential study by Guidehouse, the external consulting firm that completed the
9    original study for the 2021 IRP.

10   The update incorporated BC Hydro’s April 2023 Reference Load Forecast, new
11   demand response measures, insights from BC Hydro’s program activity, and
12   Guidehouse’s subject-matter expertise.

13   The assessment was carried out using Guidehouse’s DRSim (Demand Response
14   Simulation) model, which was customized to represent BC Hydro’s customer base
15   and characteristics. The model considered a broad range of measures applicable to
16   various market segments.

17   The analysis followed a structured approach. First, Guidehouse segmented the
18   market by customer class and region, and developed baseline projections of peak
19   consumption calibrated to BC Hydro’s load forecast, and customer end-use and
20   technology shares. Next, the demand response measures were defined and
21   assumptions for each measure were developed, including participation levels.
22   Finally, peak load reductions for each measure were calculated and aggregated to
23   produce an overall trajectory of capacity savings and costs over time.

24   Key assumptions in the updated study are shown in Table J-1 below.

7    For Demand Response B, Guidehouse provided input on how increased incentives
8    might affect participation. Guidehouse noted that the relationship between incentives
9    and participation is typically non-linear and varies significantly across jurisdictions. At

11   analysis could result in approximately a 15% increase in participation9 compared to
12   Demand Response Programs A. BC Hydro used these assumptions to develop
13   Demand Response Programs B.

14   1.3             Customer Solar
15   BC Hydro engaged Dunsky Energy + Climate Advisors to assess the potential of
16   behind-the-meter customer solar generation to inform resource options for the
17   2025 IRP. The study utilized Dunsky’s Solar Adoption Model (SAM), incorporating
18   British Columbia (B.C.)-specific inputs to forecast adoption and corresponding load
19   impacts under various scenarios reflecting different market and policy conditions.

20   The study10 characterized the market in BC Hydro’s service territory according to
21   geographic region, sector, and rate class for the residential and general service

     8    Demand Response A is an initiated resource, aligned with the demand response resource options selected
          in the Updated 2021 IRP. Demand Response B is a resource option that includes the same measures as
          Demand Response A but reflects a doubling of incentive levels.
     9    There is uncertainty with this estimate, since demand response is relatively new to the B.C. market, and our
          programs are in early stages of ramp up. We expect to gain more insights on the relationship between
          incentive levels and participation in demand response programs over time as our programs become more
          established.
     10   The Dunsky Market Potential Report was included as Appendix B-1 in BC Hydro’s Net Metering Evidentiary
          Update, Exhibit B-8, of BC Hydro’s Net Metering Service Rate Application:



                              BC Hydro 2025 Integrated Resource Plan Application
                                                                                                               Page 5

                                                                  Demand-Side Measures Key Assumptions




1    categories. It then estimated the technical potential – the estimated theoretical
2    maximum deployment of solar – based on building stock, site suitability, and solar
3    generation profiles.

4    The SAM was calibrated to local market characteristics using historical data on
5    market size, electricity rates, excess generation rates, system costs, and available
6    incentives. Economic curve parameters representing the local population’s
7    willingness to pay for solar and expected levels of return that would encourage
8    adoption were calibrated to the local market. In addition, diffusion curve parameters
9    were calibrated. These parameters capture local market barriers and the degree to
10   which the market adopts new technologies over time, accounting for local
11   demographics and composition of market segments and their varying motivation for
12   adoption.

13   Achievable potential was then estimated as a function of customer economics and
14   technology diffusion theory in the calibrated model for each scenario, based on
15   scenario specific inputs.

16   The customer solar resource options included in the 2025 IRP are:

17   •      Customer Solar A is based on the Incentive Program scenario11 from the
18          Dunsky potential assessment and assumes incentive levels at 33% of the
19          customer cost; and

20   •      Customer Solar B is based on the Enhanced Economics scenario12 from the
21          Dunsky potential assessment and is an increment to Customer Solar A. It
22          assumes incentive levels at 50% of the customer cost.


          https://docs.bcuc.com/documents/proceedings/2025/doc_80685_b-8-bch-netmetering-evidentiary-
          update.pdf.
     11   The Incentive Program scenario is based on an illustrative version of BC Hydro’s Self-Generation Service
          Rate and BC Hydro incentives for solar and battery storage along with marketing activities.
     12   The Enhanced Economics is based on the Incentive Program scenario but with higher incentive levels and
          additional marketing activities.
